# How to use this guide

Adult Health Nursing I is the largest clinical nursing subject in Semester 3 of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing programme. It integrates pathophysiology, medical management and nursing care across nine body systems and runs through approximately **115 theory hours plus extensive clinical hours**. Everything you learn here directly supports your clinical postings in medical and surgical wards.

## Exam pattern

**Standard INC 75-mark end-semester theory paper, 3 hours.** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 20 objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — answer 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — answer 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

AHN-I also carries **50 marks of internal assessment** (sessional, assignments, clinical log) which are added to the university marks. The practical examination is separate.

## How the nine unit files map to the INC syllabus

The INC syllabus for AHN-I has nine numbered units. Each notes file covers one INC unit:

| Notes file | INC unit | Main content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 | I | Introduction to medical-surgical nursing, asepsis, wound care, peri-operative care, fluids and electrolytes, shock and pain management |
| Unit 2 | II | Intraoperative care and anaesthesia; BCLS/BLS |
| Unit 3 | III | Respiratory disorders (pneumonia, COPD, tuberculosis, asthma, pleural effusion, lung cancer) |
| Unit 4 | IV | Digestive system disorders (peptic ulcer, IBD, cirrhosis, hepatitis, pancreatitis, GI cancers) |
| Unit 5 | V | Cardiovascular disorders with BCLS/BLS (IHD, MI, heart failure, hypertension, DVT, PE) |
| Unit 6 | VI | Blood disorders and endocrine disorders (anaemia, haematological cancers, diabetes, thyroid) |
| Unit 7 | VII | Integumentary system (eczema, psoriasis, pressure ulcers, burns, skin infections, skin cancers) |
| Unit 8 | VIII | Musculoskeletal disorders (fractures, osteomyelitis, osteoporosis, RA, OA, back pain) |
| Unit 9 | IX | Communicable diseases (HIV/AIDS, TB, hepatitis, malaria, typhoid, dengue) |

Revise each notes file alongside your clinical posting for that system.

## How to study this subject

AHN-I is wide; you cannot memorise everything the week before the exam. Use this strategy:

1. **Read the unit notes** while you have that posting — clinical experience makes the notes memorable.
2. **Learn the nursing care plan frame** for every condition: assessment → nursing diagnosis → goal → interventions → evaluation. Every long and short essay benefits from this structure.
3. **Learn procedures and investigations** in the clinical area: IV cannulation, dressings, catheterisation, oxygen delivery, ECG. The viva and practical exams test these directly.
4. **Answer the questions in the question bank** after each unit; check the full answer structure rather than just the main points.
5. **Run the MCQ bank** before class tests and again before the exam.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most years; often as a long essay or a short answer; learn the full nursing care plan.
- **Medium** — appears every few years or as part of a broader question.
- **Low** — less common, but tested in MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from the typical pattern of INC nursing papers; they are not a promise.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Introduction, wounds, fluids, shock | Types of wounds and healing, wound dressing procedure, IV fluid types (crystalloids vs colloids), types of shock and their nursing management, pain assessment (VAS, numerical scale) |
| 2 Intraoperative and anaesthesia | Pre-operative assessment and preparation (consent, bowel prep, NBM), post-anaesthesia recovery, BCLS steps (CAB — compressions 30:2 at 100–120/min) |
| 3 Respiratory | Nursing care of pneumonia, COPD vs asthma, chest physiotherapy, oxygen therapy types, monitoring SpO2, care of chest drain (underwater seal drainage) |
| 4 Digestive | Peptic ulcer (gastric vs duodenal), liver cirrhosis, care of patient with ascites (paracentesis), nursing care of jaundice, nasogastric tube feeding |
| 5 Cardiovascular | Myocardial infarction nursing care (MONA — morphine, oxygen, nitrates, aspirin), heart failure (upright position, oxygen, fluid restriction), hypertension patient education, DVT prevention |
| 6 Blood and endocrine | Anaemia (types, iron-deficiency management), diabetic patient education (foot care, insulin injection technique, hypoglycaemia recognition and management) |
| 7 Integumentary | Pressure ulcer stages, Braden scale, pressure ulcer prevention (5 Ps), burns classification, Parkland formula, nursing care of a burn patient |
| 8 Musculoskeletal | Types of fractures, 5 Ps neurovascular check, cast care, compartment syndrome (emergency), RA vs OA comparison, osteoporosis prevention |
| 9 Communicable diseases | HIV nursing care (standard precautions, ART adherence, PEP after needle-stick), TB DOTS regimen and airborne precautions, dengue warning signs, typhoid complications |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Start every answer with a nursing assessment.** The nursing process always begins with assessment, and examiners reward it. A one-line definition + assessment + relevant history and physical findings sets up a strong answer.

2. **Use the nursing process frame explicitly.** Structure every nursing care answer as: Assessment → Nursing diagnoses → Goals/outcomes → Nursing interventions → Evaluation. This applies to both long essays and short answers.

3. **Classify before you describe.** For fractures, anaemia, hepatitis, malaria, shock — give the classification table first. Classification alone is worth 2–3 marks in a 10-mark essay.

4. **Write nursing interventions with rationale.** For example: "Elevate the limb (to reduce swelling and improve venous return)." A bare list of interventions scores less than a list with reasons.

5. **Quote normal values when relevant.** Hb normal ranges, SpO2 targets, BP targets, urine output targets (0.5 mL/kg/h), blood sugar ranges. These show clinical reasoning.

6. **For BCLS questions**, write the exact sequence: Check safety → Unresponsive? → Shout for help → Call emergency (activate code) → Check pulse (<10 seconds) → Start compressions 30:2, rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm → AED as soon as available. Never say "give CPR" without the sequence.

7. **Tables score well for comparisons.** RA vs OA, gastric vs duodenal ulcer, types of hepatitis, types of shock, degrees of burns — write comparisons as tables; they are easy to read and mark.

8. **Health education and discharge teaching** are frequently asked. Always include in a nursing care essay.

9. **For very short answers (2 marks)**, give a one-line definition or classification plus one nursing point. Do not write a paragraph.

# Last-night revision sheet

Adult Health Nursing I is a 75-mark end-semester paper (20 MCQ + 2 × 10 long essays + 7 × 5 short answers). If you have one hour, work through the comparison tables and procedure sequences below.

---

**Wound healing phases**

| Phase | Timing | Key events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemostasis | Minutes | Vasoconstriction → platelet plug → clot |
| Inflammatory | Days 1–5 | Vasodilation, WBC migration, wound debridement; red, warm, swollen |
| Proliferative | Days 6 – weeks 3 | Granulation tissue, fibroplasia, angiogenesis, wound contraction, epithelialisation |
| Remodelling | 3 weeks – 2 years | Collagen remodelling, scar matures; tensile strength peaks at ~80% of normal |

First intention (sutured clean wound) → thin scar. Second intention (open wound) → granulation → larger scar.

---

**Burns**

Rule of nines (adult): head + neck = 9%, each arm = 9%, anterior trunk = 18%, posterior trunk = 18%, each leg = 18%, perineum = 1%. Children: use Lund–Browder (head is larger).

| Depth | Features | Healing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Superficial (1st degree) | Red, dry, painful | 3–5 days, no scar |
| Superficial partial (2nd, superficial) | Pink, blistered, very painful | 10–14 days |
| Deep partial (2nd, deep) | Pale/white, less painful | 3–8 weeks, scarring |
| Full thickness (3rd degree) | Waxy/leathery/charred, **painless** | Needs skin graft |

**Parkland formula**: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA of Hartmann's in 24 h. Half in first 8 hours (from time of burn), half over next 16 hours. Target urine output: 0.5–1 mL/kg/h.

---

**Pressure ulcer stages (NPUAP)**

| Stage | Features |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Non-blanchable erythema, skin intact |
| 2 | Partial-thickness; shallow open ulcer / blister |
| 3 | Full-thickness into subcutaneous fat; no exposed bone |
| 4 | Full-thickness with exposed bone, tendon or muscle |

Prevention — 5 Ps: Position (2-hourly turns), Pressure-relieving mattress, Proper skin care, Protein (nutrition), Patient education. Braden score ≤18 = at risk.

---

**Fracture healing stages**

```text
Haematoma (hours) → Soft callus (1–2 weeks) → Hard callus (3–6 weeks) → Remodelling (months–years)
```

Compartment syndrome: pain unrelieved by analgesia + tense limb + paraesthesia = **emergency** → bivalve cast → surgeon → fasciotomy.

5 Ps neurovascular check: **P**ain, **P**ulse, **P**allor, **P**araesthesia, **P**aralysis. Check every 1–2 hours post-fracture/cast.

---

**RA vs OA**

| Feature | Rheumatoid arthritis | Osteoarthritis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Autoimmune synovitis | Cartilage degeneration |
| Joints | Symmetric; small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists) | Asymmetric; weight-bearing (knee, hip) |
| Morning stiffness | >1 hour | <30 minutes |
| Systemic features | Yes (fatigue, anaemia, nodules) | No |
| RF | Positive (~70%) | Negative |
| Treatment | DMARDs (methotrexate) | NSAIDs, physiotherapy, weight loss |

---

**HIV stages**

| Stage | CD4 | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary infection | Variable | Seroconversion illness |
| Asymptomatic | >500 → falling | No symptoms; contagious |
| Symptomatic | 350–200 | Oral candida, shingles, weight loss |
| AIDS | <200 | PCP, cryptococcal meningitis, Kaposi's sarcoma |

ART drug classes: NRTIs (tenofovir/3TC), NNRTIs (efavirenz), PIs (lopinavir), INSTIs (dolutegravir). India first line: TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir). U = U (undetectable = untransmittable).

Needle-stick: wash + report + PEP within **72 hours**.

---

**TB reminders**

Organism: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, AFB, airborne transmission.
Diagnosis: sputum AFB smear × 3, Xpert MTB/RIF, chest X-ray (upper lobe cavitation), Mantoux (>10 mm = positive for most).
Regimen: **2HRZE/4HR** under DOTS. Rifampicin → orange urine/tears (normal, warn patient). Isoniazid → give pyridoxine to prevent neuropathy. Ethambutol → monthly vision check.
Isolation: airborne precautions (N95 for staff, surgical mask on patient).

---

**Hepatitis comparison**

| Type | Route | Chronic? | Vaccine? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Faeco-oral | No | Yes |
| B | Blood, sexual, MTCT | Yes (~10% adults) | Yes (3-dose) |
| C | Blood | Yes (~80%) | No (treat with DAAs) |
| D | Blood (needs HBV) | Yes | HBV vaccine covers D |
| E | Faeco-oral | No (usually) | Yes (India) |

HBV vaccine: birth, 6 w, 10 w, 14 w in India. HBsAg+ mother: baby gets HBV vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours.

---

**BCLS sequence**

```text
1. Check safety
2. Unresponsive? Shout for help
3. Call emergency services / activate code
4. Check pulse (<10 seconds)
5. 30 compressions (rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, full recoil)
6. 2 rescue breaths (or compression-only if untrained)
7. AED as soon as available → analyse → shock if advised
Continue until ROSC, AED takes over, or told to stop
```

**MONA for MI**: Morphine (pain), Oxygen (SpO2 <94%), Nitrates (sublingual), Aspirin (300 mg stat).

---

**Normal values to quote**

| Parameter | Normal |
| --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | Men 13–17 g/dL; women 12–15 g/dL |
| Total WBC | 4,000–11,000 /µL |
| Platelets | 1.5–4.5 lakh /µL |
| SpO2 | 95–100% |
| Blood pressure (adult) | <120/80 mmHg (normal); ≥140/90 = hypertension |
| Fasting blood sugar | 70–100 mg/dL |
| Urine output target (post-op/burns) | 0.5–1 mL/kg/h |

---

**Exam reminder**: AHN-I is 75 marks, 3 hours. Start every answer with nursing assessment. Use the nursing process frame. Classify before describing. Write comparisons as tables. BCLS in exact sequence. Parkland formula: 4 × kg × %TBSA.

# Unit 1: Introduction, asepsis, wound care, peri-operative care, fluid and electrolytes, shock and pain

This notes file covers INC Unit I (Introduction, 6 hours) and INC Unit III (common signs and symptoms — fluid and electrolyte imbalance, shock and pain, 6 hours). Both units give you the basic ideas you will use in every later system: the nursing process, asepsis, wound healing, pre- and post-operative care, fluids, shock and pain.

## 1.1 Evolution and trends of medical-surgical nursing

Medical-surgical nursing (now called adult health nursing) is the care of adults with illness or injury that is treated with medicines (medical) or with operations (surgical).

| Period | What changed |
| --- | --- |
| Early times | Care given by family members and religious orders; little knowledge of disease |
| Florence Nightingale (1850s) | Cleanliness, ventilation, nutrition and observation; nursing as a trained calling |
| Late 19th–early 20th century | Germ theory, antisepsis and anaesthesia make surgery safer; nurses assist in theatres |
| Mid 20th century | Antibiotics, intensive care units, specialised wards (cardiac, renal, neuro) |
| Present | Evidence-based practice, nursing process, critical care, day-care surgery, minimally invasive surgery, telehealth, nurse practitioners, patient safety programmes |

**Current trends**

- Shorter hospital stay and day-care (ambulatory) surgery → more discharge teaching and home care.
- Specialisation: critical care, oncology, cardiac, nephrology, orthopaedic nursing.
- Evidence-based practice and clinical protocols (care bundles, checklists).
- Patient safety: surgical safety checklist, infection-control programmes, fall prevention.
- Use of computers, electronic records and monitoring equipment.
- Holistic care, rehabilitation, palliative care and respect for patients' rights.

## 1.2 International classification of diseases (ICD)

- The **International Classification of Diseases** is published by the World Health Organization (WHO). It gives each disease and health problem a code, so that records from any hospital or country can be compared.
- Uses: hospital records, death and illness statistics, planning of services, research, insurance and billing.
- The current revision is **ICD-11** (in use from 2022); many Indian hospitals still use ICD-10 codes. Check which version your hospital record room uses.
- Nurse's part: write the diagnosis clearly and completely so that it can be coded correctly.

## 1.3 Roles and responsibilities of the nurse in medical-surgical settings

| Setting | Main roles |
| --- | --- |
| **Outpatient department (OPD)** | Receive and register patients, triage (who needs care first), check vital signs, weight and history, prepare for examination, assist in minor procedures, give injections and dressings, health education, follow-up advice and referral |
| **In-patient unit (ward)** | Admission and orientation, assessment, nursing care plan, giving medicines, monitoring, preparing for investigations and surgery, preventing complications (falls, pressure ulcers, infection), recording, discharge planning and teaching |
| **Intensive care unit (ICU)** | Continuous monitoring (ECG, saturation, blood pressure), care of ventilated patients, infusion pumps, emergency drugs and defibrillation, strict asepsis, family support, early detection of deterioration |

General roles in all settings: care giver, educator, counsellor, advocate, coordinator of the health team, manager, researcher.

### The nursing process (used throughout this course)

```text
 Assessment → Nursing diagnosis → Planning (goals) → Implementation → Evaluation
      ↑                                                                    │
      └───────────────────── reassess and modify ──────────────────────────┘
```

- **Assessment**: history, physical examination, investigation results.
- **Nursing diagnosis**: a statement of the patient's response to illness, e.g. "Ineffective airway clearance related to thick secretions as shown by noisy breathing and ineffective cough".
- **Planning**: list problems by priority (airway, breathing, circulation first), set measurable goals.
- **Implementation**: nursing actions with rationale.
- **Evaluation**: was the goal met? If not, change the plan.

## 1.4 Medical and surgical asepsis

**Asepsis** means freedom from disease-causing micro-organisms.

| Medical asepsis (clean technique) | Surgical asepsis (sterile technique) |
| --- | --- |
| Reduces the number and spread of micro-organisms | Removes all micro-organisms and spores from an area or object |
| Hand hygiene, clean gloves, cleaning, isolation, waste disposal | Sterile gloves, gowns, instruments, sterile field |
| Used for routine care, oral care, giving oral drugs | Used for surgery, catheterisation, dressings of surgical wounds, injections, IV lines |

**Principles of surgical asepsis**

1. Only sterile objects touch a sterile field.
2. If in doubt about sterility, consider it unsterile.
3. Sterile objects are kept above waist level and in sight.
4. A sterile field becomes contaminated if wet (strike-through).
5. The 2.5 cm border of a sterile drape is considered unsterile.
6. Do not talk, cough or reach across a sterile field.
7. Sterile persons face each other and face the sterile field.

### Inflammation

Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection.

- **Cardinal signs**: redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), pain (dolor) and loss of function.
- **Vascular events**: brief narrowing of vessels → widening (vasodilatation) → more blood flow (redness, heat) → vessels become leaky → fluid and protein leave (swelling).
- **Cellular events**: white cells (first neutrophils, later macrophages) stick to the vessel wall, move out and eat bacteria and debris (phagocytosis).
- **Acute inflammation** lasts days; **chronic inflammation** lasts weeks to months, with lymphocytes, macrophages and fibrosis.

### Infection

Infection is the invasion and multiplication of micro-organisms that harm the body.

```text
Chain of infection:
 Infectious agent → Reservoir → Portal of exit → Mode of transmission
       → Portal of entry → Susceptible host → (back to agent)
```

Breaking any link prevents spread: hand hygiene breaks transmission; immunisation protects the host; cleaning removes the reservoir.

Signs of local wound infection: increasing pain, redness spreading, swelling, warmth, pus, foul smell, wound opening. General signs: fever, rapid pulse, raised white cell count.

## 1.5 Wound healing

A **wound** is a break in the continuity of skin or tissue.

### Types of healing

| Type | How it heals | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary intention** | Clean wound with edges brought together by sutures; little scar | Clean surgical incision |
| **Secondary intention** | Wound left open, fills from the base with granulation tissue; larger scar, slower | Infected wound, pressure ulcer, burns |
| **Tertiary intention (delayed primary closure)** | Left open for a few days (to drain infection), then closed | Contaminated traumatic wound |

### Stages of wound healing

| Stage | Time (approx.) | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Haemostasis | Minutes | Vessels narrow, platelets plug, clot forms |
| 2. Inflammatory | Up to about 4–6 days | Redness, swelling; neutrophils and macrophages clean the wound |
| 3. Proliferative (granulation) | About day 4 to 3 weeks | Fibroblasts make collagen, new capillaries form (red granulation tissue), epithelium covers the wound, wound contracts |
| 4. Maturation (remodelling) | 3 weeks to a year or more | Collagen reorganises, scar becomes pale and stronger |

### Factors affecting wound healing

- **Age**: older people heal more slowly.
- **Nutrition**: protein, vitamin C, zinc and calories are needed for collagen and new cells.
- **Blood supply and oxygen**: poor circulation, anaemia, smoking delay healing.
- **Infection**: prolongs inflammation.
- **Diseases**: diabetes mellitus, cancer, kidney failure, jaundice.
- **Drugs**: corticosteroids, anticancer drugs, immunosuppressants.
- **Obesity**: fatty tissue has poor blood supply; more tension on wound.
- **Local factors**: foreign body, dead tissue, tension on suture line, movement, oedema.

### Complications of wounds

- Haemorrhage, haematoma.
- Infection and abscess.
- **Dehiscence**: partial or full separation of wound layers.
- **Evisceration**: abdominal organs come out through the opened wound — an emergency: cover with sterile saline-soaked dressing, position with knees flexed, inform surgeon.
- Keloid and hypertrophic scar, contracture, incisional hernia, fistula.

## 1.6 Wound care and dressing technique

**Purposes of dressing**: protect from contamination and injury, absorb drainage, keep wound moist for healing, apply pressure, support or immobilise, apply medication, comfort.

**Types of dressing**: dry dressing, wet-to-dry (for debridement), moist dressings (hydrocolloid, hydrogel, foam, alginate), transparent film, pressure dressing.

### Procedure: surgical wound dressing (steps with rationale)

1. Check the doctor's order and the plan of care. — *Some wounds need special solutions or must not be disturbed.*
2. Explain the procedure; give pain relief if ordered before the dressing. — *Reduces anxiety and pain; gains cooperation.*
3. Arrange privacy; position the patient comfortably with the wound exposed. — *Dignity and easy access.*
4. Perform hand hygiene; wear clean gloves and remove the soiled dressing, peeling towards the wound. — *Prevents cross-infection and avoids pulling on the wound edges.*
5. Look at the old dressing (amount, colour, smell of drainage); discard it in the correct waste bag. — *Assessment and biomedical waste segregation.*
6. Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, open the sterile dressing pack and put on sterile gloves (or use sterile forceps). — *Surgical asepsis.*
7. Assess the wound: size, edges, colour of tissue, drainage, suture line, signs of infection. — *Detects complications early.*
8. Clean with the ordered solution (often normal saline), one swab for one stroke, **from the cleanest area to the less clean**: from the incision line outward; for a drain site, in circles from the drain outward. — *Prevents carrying organisms into the wound.*
9. Dry the area, apply ordered medication and a sterile dressing; secure with tape or bandage. — *Protection and absorption.*
10. Dispose of waste correctly, clean equipment, perform hand hygiene. — *Infection control.*
11. Record: date, time, wound condition, drainage, dressing used and the patient's response. — *Legal record and continuity of care.*

**Wound drains**: open (Penrose) or closed suction (e.g. Jackson-Pratt, Romovac). Keep closed drains compressed for suction, record amount and type of drainage, keep the bag below the wound level.

## 1.7 Care of the surgical patient

Peri-operative care has three phases: **pre-operative** (from decision for surgery to arrival in theatre), **intra-operative** (Unit 2) and **post-operative** (from recovery room until full recovery).

### Pre-operative care

**Psychological preparation**: explain the surgery and what the patient will feel; answer questions; reduce fear; involve the family; respect religious wishes.

**Informed consent**: the surgeon explains the operation, risks, benefits and alternatives; the patient (adult, conscious, not sedated) signs freely; the nurse checks that the form is signed and witnessed. For a minor or an unconscious patient, the parent or legal guardian signs; in a life-threatening emergency, hospital policy is followed.

**Physical preparation**

| Area | Actions and reason |
| --- | --- |
| Assessment | History, allergies, current medicines, vital signs, weight, height |
| Investigations | Complete blood count, blood group and cross-match, blood sugar, kidney tests, ECG, chest X-ray, others as ordered |
| Nutrition | **Nil by mouth** for the period ordered (usually several hours for solids, less for clear fluids) — prevents vomiting and aspiration during anaesthesia |
| Bowel | Enema or bowel wash only if ordered (e.g. bowel surgery) |
| Skin | Bath, clean the operation site; hair removed only if needed, with clippers just before surgery, not by shaving — shaving causes small cuts that raise infection risk |
| Bladder | Ask the patient to void before going to theatre, or catheterise if ordered — an empty bladder is not injured and is out of the way |
| Valuables, prosthesis | Remove jewellery, dentures, contact lenses, hairpins, nail polish, make-up; hand over valuables — prevents loss, airway obstruction, burns from diathermy and allows nail-bed colour to be checked |
| Medicines | Give pre-medication as ordered (e.g. sedatives, anticholinergics, antacids); after sedation keep side rails up |
| Teaching | Deep breathing, coughing with splinting the wound, leg exercises, early ambulation, use of incentive spirometer |
| Identification | Identity band, site marking, checklist completed and signed |

### Post-operative care

**Immediate care (recovery room / post-anaesthesia care unit)**

1. **Airway**: position on the side or with head turned (until fully awake) to prevent tongue falling back and aspiration of vomit; keep suction ready; oral airway until gag reflex returns.
2. **Breathing**: watch rate, depth, oxygen saturation; give oxygen as ordered.
3. **Circulation**: pulse, blood pressure every 15 minutes at first; skin colour, capillary refill.
4. **Wound and drains**: look for bleeding.
5. **Level of consciousness** and return of reflexes and sensation (after spinal anaesthesia).
6. **Pain**, nausea and vomiting, temperature.
7. Discharge from recovery when stable and awake (using a scoring system such as the Aldrete score).

**Care in the ward**

- Vital signs as ordered; intake and output.
- Pain relief as ordered and regular pain assessment.
- Early ambulation as soon as allowed — prevents deep vein thrombosis, chest infection, constipation and urinary retention.
- Deep breathing, coughing and incentive spirometry every hour while awake.
- Diet: sips of water → liquids → soft → normal diet when bowel sounds return and as ordered.
- Wound care, drain care, catheter care.
- Hygiene, mouth care, positioning and pressure-area care.

### Post-operative complications

| Complication | Usual time | Nursing points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemorrhage, shock | First 24 hours | Rapid weak pulse, falling BP, pallor, bleeding from wound or drain → inform surgeon, lie flat with legs raised, prepare fluids/blood |
| Airway obstruction, hypoxia | Immediate | Head tilt, suction, oxygen |
| Nausea and vomiting | Early | Turn to side, antiemetics as ordered |
| Urinary retention | 6–8 hours | Palpable bladder; privacy, running water, warm bedpan; catheterise if ordered |
| Atelectasis, pneumonia | 1–3 days | Fever, crepitations; deep breathing, coughing, ambulation |
| Paralytic ileus | 1–3 days | Distension, absent bowel sounds; nil orally, nasogastric drainage |
| Wound infection | 3–7 days | Fever, redness, discharge |
| Deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism | Days 5–14 | Calf pain, swelling; leg exercises, stockings, early walking |
| Dehiscence, evisceration | 5–8 days | Often after coughing or straining |

## 1.8 Alternative therapies in medical-surgical care

Alternative and complementary therapies are used along with standard treatment, not in place of it. In India, AYUSH systems (Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy) are recognised.

Examples useful to medical-surgical patients:

- **Relaxation, breathing exercises, yoga and meditation** — reduce anxiety and pain.
- **Music therapy, guided imagery, distraction** — reduce pain and anxiety around surgery.
- **Massage, therapeutic touch** — comfort, sleep.
- **Acupressure** — some patients use it for nausea.
- **Herbal products** — ask about them in the history; some affect bleeding or interact with prescribed drugs, so the doctor must know.

Nurse's role: ask about every therapy the patient uses, respect beliefs, encourage only safe practices, and report herbal products before surgery.

## 1.9 Fluid and electrolyte imbalance

Body water is about 60% of adult body weight: two-thirds inside the cells (intracellular fluid, ICF) and one-third outside (extracellular fluid, ECF — plasma and interstitial fluid).

| Electrolyte | Normal serum value (approx.) | Main role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium (Na⁺) | 135–145 mEq/L | Main ECF ion; water balance, nerve impulses |
| Potassium (K⁺) | 3.5–5.0 mEq/L | Main ICF ion; heart rhythm, muscle contraction |
| Calcium (Ca²⁺) | 8.5–10.5 mg/dL | Bones, clotting, nerve and muscle excitability |
| Magnesium (Mg²⁺) | 1.5–2.5 mEq/L | Enzymes, nerve and muscle function |
| Chloride (Cl⁻) | 96–106 mEq/L | Follows sodium |
| Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) | 22–26 mEq/L | Acid–base buffer |

Normal values differ slightly between laboratories; always use the laboratory's own range.

### Fluid volume deficit (dehydration, hypovolaemia)

- Causes: vomiting, diarrhoea, bleeding, burns, fever and sweating, poor intake, diuretics, drains.
- Signs: thirst, dry mouth and skin, poor skin turgor, sunken eyes, weight loss, rapid weak pulse, low blood pressure, postural fall in BP, less urine (concentrated), raised haematocrit.
- Care: monitor intake and output, daily weight, vital signs; oral fluids or IV fluids as ordered; mouth care; prevent falls on standing.

### Fluid volume excess (overload)

- Causes: heart failure, kidney failure, too much IV fluid, liver cirrhosis.
- Signs: weight gain, oedema, distended neck veins, bounding pulse, high BP, breathlessness, crackles in the lungs.
- Care: fluid and salt restriction as ordered, diuretics as ordered, semi-Fowler's position, daily weight, intake and output, skin care of oedematous areas.

### Common electrolyte imbalances

| Imbalance | Common causes | Main features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hyponatraemia** | Vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, excess water | Headache, confusion, muscle cramps, seizures |
| **Hypernatraemia** | Water loss, poor intake, fever | Thirst, restlessness, confusion, dry tongue |
| **Hypokalaemia** | Vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, nasogastric suction | Muscle weakness, cramps, constipation, ileus, arrhythmias |
| **Hyperkalaemia** | Kidney failure, crushing injury, burns, excess intake | Weakness, tall peaked T waves, dangerous arrhythmias, cardiac arrest |
| **Hypocalcaemia** | After thyroid or parathyroid surgery, kidney failure | Tingling around mouth and fingers, muscle spasm (tetany), positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, seizures |
| **Hypercalcaemia** | Hyperparathyroidism, bone cancers | Weakness, constipation, kidney stones, confusion |

**Nursing point**: potassium given by vein is never given as a direct push; it is always diluted and given slowly through an infusion as ordered, with ECG monitoring if the dose is high, because a rapid rise in potassium can stop the heart.

### Intravenous therapy (overview)

| Type of fluid | Examples | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Isotonic | Normal saline (0.9% NaCl), Ringer's lactate | Replace ECF loss, shock, surgery |
| Hypotonic | 0.45% saline | Cell dehydration |
| Hypertonic | 3% saline, 10% dextrose | Special uses under close watch |

Nursing responsibilities in IV therapy: check order and fluid, asepsis, correct flow rate, watch the site for **infiltration** (cool, swollen, pale) and **phlebitis** (red, warm, painful along the vein), watch for fluid overload, change sets and dressings as per policy, record.

Flow rate (drops per minute) = (volume in mL × drop factor) ÷ time in minutes.

## 1.10 Shock

**Shock** is a life-threatening condition in which blood flow to the tissues is not enough to meet their need for oxygen, leading to cell damage.

### Types

| Type | Cause | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hypovolaemic | Loss of blood or fluid | Haemorrhage, burns, severe diarrhoea |
| Cardiogenic | Failure of the heart as a pump | Myocardial infarction |
| Obstructive | Block to filling or outflow of heart | Cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolism |
| Distributive — septic | Infection with widening of vessels | Severe infection |
| Distributive — anaphylactic | Severe allergy | Drug or insect-sting allergy |
| Distributive — neurogenic | Loss of sympathetic tone | High spinal cord injury |

### Stages

```text
 Initial → Compensatory → Progressive → Irreversible (refractory)
 (cells short   (body keeps BP     (compensation      (organ failure;
  of oxygen)     up: fast pulse,     fails: BP falls,   no response to
                 cool skin, less     acidosis, organ    treatment)
                 urine)              damage)
```

### Signs and symptoms

Restlessness and anxiety (early), rapid weak pulse, rapid breathing, cold clammy pale skin (warm and flushed in early septic shock), low blood pressure (later sign), reduced urine output (less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour), thirst, confusion, drowsiness.

### Management

- **Airway and breathing**: oxygen; prepare for ventilation if needed.
- **Circulation**: two large-bore IV cannulas; fluids and blood as ordered.
- **Position**: lie flat with legs raised (not with head injury or breathlessness).
- **Treat the cause**: stop bleeding, give antibiotics for sepsis, adrenaline for anaphylaxis as ordered, treat heart failure.
- **Drugs** (by class only): vasopressors and inotropes to support BP, as ordered.

### Nursing care

- Monitor vital signs every 15 minutes, oxygen saturation, level of consciousness.
- Hourly urine output through an indwelling catheter.
- Monitor central venous pressure if a line is in place.
- Keep warm with blankets (do not apply direct heat).
- Reassure the patient and family.
- Record intake, output and all observations.

**Nursing diagnoses**: decreased tissue perfusion; deficient fluid volume; anxiety.

## 1.11 Pain

**Pain** is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience linked with actual or possible tissue damage. Pain is whatever the patient says it is.

### Types

| Basis | Types |
| --- | --- |
| Duration | **Acute** (sudden, short, has a cause, e.g. post-operative) and **chronic** (lasts more than 3–6 months, e.g. arthritis, cancer) |
| Origin | Somatic (skin, muscle, bone), visceral (organs, poorly localised), neuropathic (nerve damage, burning or shooting), **referred** (felt away from the source, e.g. heart pain in the left arm), phantom limb pain |

### Gate control theory (simple form)

Pain signals travel to the brain through a "gate" in the spinal cord. Rubbing, massage, heat and cold stimulate large nerve fibres that close the gate; anxiety opens it; the brain can also close it (distraction, relaxation, endorphins). This explains why non-drug methods help.

### Pain assessment

Use **PQRST**:

- **P** — provoking and palliating factors (what makes it worse or better)
- **Q** — quality (sharp, dull, burning, crushing)
- **R** — region and radiation
- **S** — severity, on a scale
- **T** — timing (onset, duration, pattern)

Pain scales: numeric rating scale (0 to 10), visual analogue scale, verbal descriptor scale, Wong-Baker faces scale (children, communication problems), behavioural scales for patients who cannot speak.

Also observe: facial expression, guarding, restlessness, sweating, rapid pulse and raised BP (acute pain).

### Management

**Drug methods (classes only)**: non-opioid analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs), opioid analgesics (for severe pain), adjuvants (some antidepressants and anticonvulsants for nerve pain), local anaesthetics (nerve blocks, epidural). WHO analgesic ladder: step 1 non-opioid → step 2 weak opioid → step 3 strong opioid, each with or without adjuvants. Patient-controlled analgesia is used after major surgery.

**Non-drug methods**: positioning and support, splinting the wound while coughing, heat or cold as ordered, massage, relaxation and breathing, distraction, music, guided imagery, TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation).

**Nursing responsibilities**: believe the patient's report; assess before and after each intervention; give analgesics on time and before pain becomes severe; watch for side effects of opioids (breathing slowing, drowsiness, constipation, nausea); record the pain score as the "fifth vital sign".

**Nursing diagnosis example**: Acute pain related to surgical incision as shown by pain score 7/10 and guarding of the abdomen. Goal: pain score below 3/10 within one hour.

## Remember

- Nursing process: assessment → diagnosis → planning → implementation → evaluation.
- ICD is published by WHO; current version ICD-11.
- Five signs of inflammation: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function.
- Healing: primary (clean, sutured), secondary (open, granulation), tertiary (delayed closure).
- Stages: haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation → maturation.
- Clean a wound from clean to less clean, one swab per stroke.
- Evisceration: cover with sterile saline-soaked dressing, knees flexed, call surgeon.
- Pre-op: consent, nil by mouth, skin preparation with clippers, empty bladder, remove dentures and jewellery, teach exercises.
- Post-op priorities: airway, breathing, circulation; watch for haemorrhage and shock.
- Potassium is never given IV push.
- Hypocalcaemia → tetany, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs.
- Shock: low BP is a late sign; restlessness and fast pulse come early; urine < 0.5 mL/kg/h.
- Pain is what the patient says it is; assess with PQRST and a 0–10 scale.

# Unit 2: Intraoperative care and anaesthesia

This notes file covers INC Unit II (Intraoperative care, 15 hours). It deals with the operation theatre (OT), the OT team, positioning and draping, instruments and sutures, sterilisation, scrubbing, monitoring, safety, anaesthesia and legal aspects.

## 2.1 Organisation and physical set-up of the operation theatre

### Classification of operation theatres

- **By type of surgery**: general, orthopaedic, cardiothoracic, neurosurgical, obstetric and gynaecological, eye, ENT, emergency (trauma) theatre, day-care theatre.
- **By cleanliness of procedures**: clean (e.g. hernia repair), clean-contaminated (e.g. gall bladder, bowel opened under control), contaminated (e.g. fresh trauma, spillage from bowel), dirty/infected (e.g. abscess, perforated bowel). Dirty cases are often listed last or done in a separate theatre.
- **By design**: single-theatre unit or a theatre complex with several theatres sharing common areas.

### OT design — the zones

The OT complex is planned so that people and articles move from clean to cleaner areas and never back the wrong way.

| Zone | Areas | Who and what |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Protective (outer) zone** | Reception, waiting, changing rooms, stores, patient transfer area | Street clothes allowed up to the changing room |
| **Clean zone** | Pre-operative (holding) area, recovery room, staff rest room, corridors | Theatre clothes required |
| **Aseptic (sterile) zone** | Operating rooms, scrub area, sterile stores, set-up room | Theatre clothes, cap, mask; scrubbed staff only near the sterile field |
| **Disposal zone** | Dirty utility, sluice, waste and linen collection | Used items leave by a separate route |

**Features of the operating room**

- Away from main traffic; near surgical wards, ICU, blood bank, central sterile supply department (CSSD), radiology.
- Smooth, washable, non-porous walls and floors with rounded corners; anti-static flooring.
- Positive-pressure ventilation with filtered air (HEPA filters in many theatres) and frequent air changes; air flows from clean areas out to less clean areas.
- Temperature about 20–24 °C and relative humidity about 50–60% (check your hospital standard).
- Shadowless operating lamp; emergency power supply.
- Doors kept closed; minimum movement of staff.

### Staffing and members of the OT team

| Sterile (scrubbed) members | Non-sterile (unscrubbed) members |
| --- | --- |
| Surgeon | Anaesthetist (anaesthesiologist) |
| Assistant surgeon | Circulating nurse |
| Scrub nurse (instrument nurse) | Anaesthesia technician, OT technician, perfusionist (cardiac surgery), radiographer, attendants, housekeeping |

OT nursing staff include the OT in-charge (nursing sister), scrub nurses, circulating nurses, recovery-room nurses and CSSD staff.

## 2.2 Duties and responsibilities of the nurse in the OT

### Scrub nurse

1. Prepares the instrument trolley and sterile field before the case.
2. Scrubs, gowns and gloves; helps the surgeon to gown and glove.
3. Counts swabs (sponges), needles and instruments with the circulating nurse **before the first incision, before closing a cavity, before skin closure and at the end**.
4. Passes instruments, sutures and swabs to the surgeon in the correct way (handle first, ready for use).
5. Anticipates the surgeon's needs and keeps the field tidy and sterile.
6. Takes care of specimens handed over.
7. Applies the dressing at the end and removes used instruments safely.

### Circulating nurse

1. Checks the OT (cleaning, equipment, suction, diathermy, light) before the case.
2. Receives the patient and checks identity, consent, site marking, nil-by-mouth status, allergies, investigations, prosthesis and jewellery removed.
3. Helps the anaesthetist and helps to position the patient.
4. Opens sterile packs for the scrub nurse; ties gowns.
5. Counts with the scrub nurse and records the counts.
6. Labels and sends specimens.
7. Watches for breaks in asepsis; controls traffic and noise.
8. Records the intra-operative notes and leads parts of the surgical safety checklist.
9. Transfers the patient to the recovery room with a handover.

### Scrub nurse vs circulating nurse

| Point | Scrub nurse | Circulating nurse |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sterility | Sterile (scrubbed) | Not sterile |
| Works within | Sterile field | Whole room, outside the sterile field |
| Main task | Instruments, sutures, swabs to surgeon | Supplies, patient safety, records, coordination |
| Counts | Shares counts | Shares counts and records them |

## 2.3 WHO surgical safety checklist

The checklist has three parts:

| Phase | When | Main checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sign in** | Before induction of anaesthesia | Identity, site, procedure and consent confirmed; site marked; anaesthesia machine and medicines checked; pulse oximeter on; known allergy; difficult airway or aspiration risk; risk of blood loss |
| **Time out** | Before skin incision | Team members introduce themselves; confirm patient, site and procedure; antibiotic given in time if needed; critical events reviewed; essential imaging displayed |
| **Sign out** | Before the patient leaves the theatre | Name of procedure recorded; instrument, swab and needle counts correct; specimen labelled; equipment problems noted; key concerns for recovery handed over |

The nurse documents and signs the checklist.

## 2.4 Positions and draping for common surgical procedures

| Position | How | Used for | Nursing precautions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Supine (dorsal recumbent)** | On the back, arms on arm boards (less than 90°) or at the side | Abdominal, chest, many others | Pad heels and back of head; arms not beyond 90° (brachial plexus injury) |
| **Trendelenburg** | Supine, head lower than feet | Pelvic and lower abdominal surgery | Watch breathing (abdominal organs press on diaphragm) |
| **Reverse Trendelenburg** | Head higher than feet | Upper abdominal, head and neck surgery | Footboard to stop sliding |
| **Lithotomy** | Supine, legs raised and abducted in stirrups | Perineal, vaginal, rectal, cystoscopy | Raise and lower **both legs together** slowly; pad the knees (peroneal nerve); watch BP when lowering |
| **Prone** | Face down, chest supported | Spine, back of legs, buttocks | Protect eyes, face and breasts; chest rolls for breathing; arms carefully placed |
| **Lateral (Sims' / kidney)** | On the side; kidney bridge raised | Kidney, chest (thoracotomy), hip | Pillow between legs; axillary roll; secure with straps |
| **Sitting / Fowler's** | Sitting up | Some neck, shoulder and brain surgery | Watch for low BP and air embolism |
| **Jack-knife (Kraske)** | Prone, hips raised, head and feet down | Anal and rectal surgery (piles, fissure) | Pad pressure points; watch breathing |

General rules: enough staff to move the patient; keep body alignment; pad bony points; avoid pressure on nerves and eyes; keep limbs secure; expose only the area needed; keep the patient warm.

**Draping**: sterile drapes cover the patient leaving only the operation site exposed. The scrub nurse hands drapes folded so they can be opened without touching unsterile areas; a drape once placed is not moved towards the incision.

## 2.5 Instruments, sutures and equipment

### Basic instrument groups

| Group | Examples | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cutting | Scalpel (Bard-Parker handle with blades), scissors (Mayo, Metzenbaum) | Cut tissue and sutures |
| Grasping and holding | Tissue forceps (toothed and non-toothed), Allis, Babcock, Kocher's | Hold tissue |
| Clamping (haemostats) | Artery forceps (straight and curved, mosquito) | Stop bleeding |
| Retracting | Langenbeck, Deaver, Morris, self-retaining retractors | Hold wound open |
| Suturing | Needle holder, needles | Sew tissue |
| Suction | Yankauer, Poole suction tips | Remove blood and fluid |
| Others | Sponge-holding forceps, towel clips, probes, dilators | Various |

### Sutures and suture materials

| Classification | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Absorbable** | Catgut (now rarely used), polyglactin (Vicryl), polyglycolic acid, polydioxanone (PDS) | Broken down in the body; used for deeper layers and bowel |
| **Non-absorbable** | Silk, nylon, polypropylene (Prolene), stainless steel wire | Stay permanently or are removed (skin) |
| Monofilament | Nylon, polypropylene | Less tissue drag, less infection |
| Multifilament (braided) | Silk, polyglactin | Easy to handle, knot well |

Other closure methods: staples, skin adhesives, adhesive strips.

**Needles**: round-bodied (for soft tissue like bowel), cutting and reverse-cutting (for skin and tough tissue); straight or curved; eyed or eyeless (swaged, suture fused to needle).

Suture size: the more zeros, the finer the thread (e.g. 6-0 is finer than 2-0).

### Equipment

Operating table, shadowless lamp, anaesthesia machine, suction machine, electrosurgical (diathermy) unit, monitors (ECG, pulse oximetry, BP, capnography), defibrillator, warming blanket, tourniquet, image intensifier.

**Diathermy safety**: place the patient (return) plate on a clean, dry, hairless, fleshy area close to the site; patient must not touch metal; no pooled spirit-based skin preparation under the patient (fire risk).

## 2.6 Disinfection and sterilisation of equipment

- **Sterilisation**: kills all micro-organisms including spores.
- **Disinfection**: kills most micro-organisms but not necessarily spores.
- **Spaulding classification**: critical items (enter sterile tissue — instruments) need sterilisation; semi-critical (touch mucous membrane — endoscopes) need high-level disinfection at least; non-critical (touch intact skin — BP cuff) need cleaning and low-level disinfection.

| Method | Examples / notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Steam under pressure (autoclave)** | Most common for instruments, linen, gloves; common cycles are 121 °C for about 15–30 minutes or 134 °C for a shorter time, as per the machine's validated cycle |
| Dry heat (hot-air oven) | Glassware, powders, oils |
| Ethylene oxide gas | Heat-sensitive items (plastics); items must be aerated afterwards |
| Hydrogen peroxide plasma | Heat-sensitive items; no toxic residue |
| Chemical (liquid) | Glutaraldehyde, ortho-phthalaldehyde (high-level disinfection of scopes) |
| Radiation (gamma rays) | Used by manufacturers for disposable items |

**Steps before sterilisation**: decontaminate → clean thoroughly (dirt protects organisms) → dry → inspect → pack → sterilise → store.

**Indicators**: physical (time, temperature, pressure gauges), chemical (autoclave tape and strips change colour), biological (spores, the most reliable test).

**Cleaning the OT**: damp dusting before the first case; cleaning between cases; terminal cleaning at the end of the day; weekly thorough cleaning; fumigation or other approved methods as per hospital policy.

## 2.7 Preparation of sets for common surgical procedures

A **set** (tray) is a pack of instruments needed for one procedure, wrapped, labelled and sterilised.

| Set | Typical contents |
| --- | --- |
| Basic minor set | Scalpel handle and blades, scissors, toothed and non-toothed forceps, artery forceps, needle holder, sponge holders, towel clips, gallipots, swabs |
| Laparotomy set | Basic set plus long instruments, abdominal retractors (Deaver, Morris, self-retaining), intestinal clamps, Babcock and Allis forceps, suction tip, large swabs (mops) |
| Appendicectomy, hernia sets | Basic set plus appropriate retractors and clamps |

Every set has a list inside so that counting and checking are easy.

## 2.8 Scrubbing, gowning, masking and gloving

### Surgical hand scrub (steps with rationale)

1. Put on cap (all hair covered) and mask (over nose and mouth) before scrubbing. — *Hair and droplets carry bacteria.*
2. Remove rings and watch; nails short, no nail polish or artificial nails. — *Organisms collect under rings and nails.*
3. Adjust water; wet hands and forearms, keeping **hands higher than elbows**. — *Water runs from the cleanest area (hands) to less clean (elbows).*
4. Clean under nails with a nail cleaner (first scrub of the day).
5. Scrub with antiseptic solution (e.g. chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine) each finger (four sides), palm, back of hand, forearm up to 5 cm above the elbow, for the time set by hospital policy (commonly about 3–5 minutes). Alcohol-based surgical hand rub is an approved alternative in many hospitals. — *Removes dirt and reduces skin flora.*
6. Rinse from fingertips to elbow without touching the tap or sink.
7. Enter the theatre backing through the door with hands held up in front, away from the body.
8. Dry with a sterile towel: one end for one hand and arm from fingers to elbow, the other end for the other arm.

### Gowning

Pick up the folded gown by the inside neckline, let it unfold away from the body, slip both arms into the sleeves; the circulating nurse ties the back. Only the front from chest to waist and the sleeves to about 5 cm above the elbow are considered sterile.

### Gloving

- **Closed gloving**: hands stay inside the gown cuffs while the gloves are put on — preferred, as bare hands never touch the outside of the gown or gloves.
- **Open gloving**: used for procedures like catheterisation or when changing a glove; the bare hand touches only the inside fold of the glove.

## 2.9 Monitoring the patient during the procedure

- Heart rate and ECG, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, end-tidal carbon dioxide (capnography), temperature.
- Breathing, airway pressure (ventilated patients).
- Blood loss: weigh swabs, measure suction contents.
- Urine output (if catheterised).
- Fluid and blood given.
- Position and pressure areas.
- Level of anaesthesia (by anaesthetist).

## 2.10 Maintaining a therapeutic environment in the OT

- Correct temperature and humidity; keep the patient warm (warm blankets, warmed fluids) to prevent hypothermia.
- Limit traffic; keep doors closed; minimise talking.
- Good lighting; quiet; respect for the unconscious patient's dignity.
- Proper waste disposal and cleaning between cases.

## 2.11 Assisting in major and minor operations; handling specimens

- Know the steps of the operation in order to anticipate needs.
- Pass instruments firmly into the surgeon's palm, in position of use.
- Keep sharps in a separate container; use a neutral (no-touch) zone for passing sharps.
- **Specimens**: receive in a container, label at once with name, identification number, specimen type and site, date; add the correct fixative (usually 10% formalin for histology), but send for culture or frozen section **fresh, without fixative**; fill request form; record in specimen register; hand over and get signature.

## 2.12 Prevention of accidents and hazards in the OT

| Hazard | Prevention |
| --- | --- |
| Wrong patient, wrong site, wrong procedure | Identification, site marking, surgical safety checklist |
| Retained swab or instrument | Counts, radio-opaque swabs |
| Burns (diathermy, fire) | Correct plate placement, let skin preparation dry, careful oxygen use |
| Falls from table | Safety straps, side supports, enough staff |
| Nerve injury, pressure injury | Proper positioning and padding |
| Electric shock | Earthing, equipment checks |
| Infection | Asepsis, sterilisation, traffic control |
| Needle-stick injuries to staff | No recapping, sharps containers, hands-free passing |
| Exposure to anaesthetic gases | Scavenging system |
| Radiation | Lead aprons, distance, thyroid shields |
| Hypothermia | Warming |
| Allergy (latex, drugs) | History, latex-free equipment |

## 2.13 Anaesthesia

**Anaesthesia** means loss of sensation, with or without loss of consciousness.

### Types and methods

| Type | Method | Examples / use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **General anaesthesia** | Unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia, muscle relaxation | Inhalation agents, intravenous induction agents; airway by endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask airway |
| **Regional — spinal** | Local anaesthetic into the subarachnoid space (CSF) in the lumbar region | Lower abdomen, perineum, lower limbs, caesarean section |
| **Regional — epidural** | Into the epidural space; catheter allows top-ups | Labour analgesia, post-operative pain relief |
| **Regional — nerve block** | Around a nerve or plexus | Brachial plexus block for arm surgery |
| **Local infiltration** | Into the tissue at the site | Minor procedures, suturing |
| **Topical** | Spray, gel, drops on mucous membrane or eye | Endoscopy, eye procedures |
| **Monitored sedation (conscious sedation)** | Sedatives and analgesics, patient can respond | Endoscopy, minor procedures |

### Phases and stages of general anaesthesia

- **Phases**: induction → maintenance → emergence (recovery).
- **Classical stages (Guedel)**, seen most clearly with older inhalation agents:

| Stage | Name | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Analgesia | From induction to loss of consciousness; drowsy |
| II | Excitement (delirium) | Irregular breathing, struggling, vomiting possible — avoid stimulation |
| III | Surgical anaesthesia | Regular breathing, muscles relaxed, reflexes lost; surgery done in this stage |
| IV | Medullary paralysis (overdose) | Breathing stops, circulation fails — emergency |

### Equipment and drugs (classes only)

- **Equipment**: anaesthesia machine (gas supply, flowmeters, vaporiser), breathing circuits, face masks, laryngoscope, endotracheal tubes, laryngeal mask airways, suction, monitors, defibrillator, emergency trolley.
- **Drug classes**: pre-medication (sedatives, anticholinergics to dry secretions, antiemetics, antacids); intravenous induction agents; inhalation agents; opioid analgesics; neuromuscular blocking agents (muscle relaxants) and their reversal agents; local anaesthetics; emergency drugs (vasopressors, drugs for arrhythmias).

### Complications and nursing considerations

| Type | Complications | Nursing considerations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General | Airway obstruction, aspiration, laryngospasm, hypoxia, low BP, arrhythmias, nausea and vomiting, sore throat, hypothermia, malignant hyperthermia (rare: high fever, muscle rigidity) | Nil by mouth before surgery, airway care, monitor until awake, lateral position, warmth |
| Spinal | Fall in BP, headache after dural puncture, urinary retention, high block affecting breathing | Monitor BP; keep flat as per local practice; fluids; check return of sensation and movement; check bladder |
| Epidural | Low BP, catheter migration, infection | Monitor BP and level of block; care of catheter site |
| Local | Allergy, toxicity if absorbed in excess (tingling around mouth, ringing in ears, convulsions) | Observe and report |

## 2.14 Legal aspects of OT nursing

- **Informed consent** before the procedure (Unit 1); consent is specific to the procedure.
- Correct identification and site — failure is negligence.
- Retained foreign bodies, burns, falls and wrong-site surgery lead to legal action; counts and checklists protect patients and staff.
- Accurate and timely documentation: counts, specimens, times, drugs, implants, events.
- Specimen handling: correct labelling and chain of custody.
- Confidentiality and dignity of the unconscious patient.
- Incident reporting of any error or near miss.
- Following biomedical waste management rules for OT waste.

## Remember

- OT zones: protective → clean → aseptic → disposal; movement always from clean to cleaner.
- Positive-pressure filtered ventilation; doors closed; limited traffic.
- Scrub nurse is sterile and passes instruments; circulating nurse is not sterile and coordinates.
- Counts: before incision, before closing a cavity, before skin closure, at the end.
- WHO checklist: sign in, time out, sign out.
- Lithotomy: raise and lower both legs together.
- Scrub with hands above elbows; closed gloving preferred.
- Autoclave is the commonest method of sterilisation; biological indicators are the most reliable test.
- Histology specimens in formalin; culture specimens fresh.
- Guedel stage III = surgical anaesthesia.
- Spinal anaesthesia: watch for low BP, headache and urinary retention.
