# Unit 3: Nursing management of patients with respiratory problems

This notes file covers INC Unit IV (18 hours). For each disorder learn the same frame: **definition → causes → pathophysiology (brief) → clinical features → diagnostic tests → medical and surgical management → nursing management → patient education**. Drugs are named by class only.

## 3.1 Review of anatomy and physiology

```text
 Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → main bronchi → bronchioles
   (upper airway)          (lower airway)          → alveoli (gas exchange)
```

- Right lung has 3 lobes, left lung 2 lobes. Each lung is covered by visceral pleura; the parietal pleura lines the chest wall; between them is the pleural space with a thin film of fluid and negative pressure.
- **Ventilation** (moving air), **diffusion** (O₂ and CO₂ across the alveolar wall) and **perfusion** (blood flow through lungs) are all needed for gas exchange.
- Breathing is controlled by the respiratory centre in the medulla, driven mainly by blood CO₂ level.
- Defences: hair and mucus in the nose, cilia (mucociliary escalator), cough reflex, alveolar macrophages.

## 3.2 Nursing assessment

### History

- Cough (dry or productive, duration, time of day), sputum (amount, colour, smell, blood — haemoptysis), breathlessness (dyspnoea — at rest, on exertion, lying flat = orthopnoea, waking at night), chest pain (pleuritic pain worse on breathing), wheeze, fever, weight loss, night sweats.
- Smoking history (pack-years), occupation (dust, chemicals), exposure to tuberculosis, allergy, past illnesses, family history.

### Physical assessment

| Step | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| **Inspection** | Rate, rhythm and depth of breathing, use of accessory muscles, chest shape (barrel chest), movement, cyanosis, clubbing of fingers, position the patient prefers |
| **Palpation** | Tracheal position, chest expansion, tactile vocal fremitus, tenderness |
| **Percussion** | Resonant (normal), dull (fluid, consolidation), stony dull (pleural effusion), hyper-resonant (pneumothorax, emphysema) |
| **Auscultation** | Breath sounds and added sounds |

### Breath sounds

| Sound | Description | Found in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vesicular | Soft, low-pitched; inspiration longer than expiration | Normal, over most of the lungs |
| Bronchial | Loud, hollow; expiration as long as inspiration | Normal over trachea; abnormal over the lung = consolidation |
| Bronchovesicular | In between | Normal near main bronchi |
| **Crackles (crepitations)** | Short popping sounds, mostly on inspiration | Fluid in alveoli: pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, fibrosis |
| **Wheeze** | Musical, continuous, mostly on expiration | Narrowed airways: asthma, COPD |
| **Rhonchi** | Low-pitched snoring sounds; may clear on coughing | Secretions in larger airways |
| **Pleural rub** | Grating sound | Inflamed pleura |
| **Stridor** | High-pitched sound on inspiration | Upper airway obstruction — emergency |

### Diagnostic tests and nursing responsibilities

| Test | Nursing points |
| --- | --- |
| Chest X-ray, CT scan | Remove metal objects; ask about pregnancy |
| **Sputum examination** (culture, smear for acid-fast bacilli, cytology) | Early-morning deep-cough specimen before mouth wash and before antibiotics, in a sterile container; not saliva |
| **Arterial blood gas (ABG)** | Usually radial artery; check collateral circulation (Allen's test); press the site for at least 5 minutes; send on ice if delay; note oxygen being given |
| **Pulse oximetry** | Normal SpO₂ usually 95–100%; warm finger, no nail polish |
| **Pulmonary function tests (spirometry)** | Explain the breathing effort needed; withhold bronchodilators if ordered |
| **Bronchoscopy** | Nil by mouth before; after: nil by mouth until gag reflex returns; watch for bleeding, breathing difficulty |
| **Thoracentesis (pleural tap)** | Sitting up leaning forward over a table; stay still, do not cough during needle insertion; after: watch for breathlessness (pneumothorax), record amount and colour of fluid |
| Pleural and lung biopsy, mantoux test, CBNAAT (rapid molecular TB test) | Explain and prepare as per test |

Normal ABG values (approximate): pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg; PaO₂ 80–100 mmHg; HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L.

## 3.3 Upper respiratory tract infections

| Condition | Key points | Care |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Common cold (rhinitis)** | Viral; sneezing, running nose, mild fever | Rest, fluids, steam inhalation, hand hygiene |
| **Sinusitis** | Facial pain, nasal block, purulent discharge | Steam, nasal decongestants, antibiotics if bacterial, as ordered |
| **Pharyngitis, tonsillitis** | Sore throat, fever, enlarged tonsils; streptococcal infection can lead to rheumatic fever | Warm saline gargles, fluids, complete antibiotic course; tonsillectomy for repeated attacks |
| **Laryngitis** | Hoarse voice | Voice rest, steam, no smoking |
| **Epistaxis** (nose bleed) | Often from Little's area | Sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes, cold compress; nasal packing if severe |

**After tonsillectomy**: lateral or prone position until awake; watch for bleeding (frequent swallowing is an early sign); cold fluids and soft foods; avoid red-coloured drinks (confused with blood).

## 3.4 Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

**Definition**: a common, preventable and treatable lung disease with persistent breathlessness and airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. It includes **chronic bronchitis** and **emphysema**. (Bronchial asthma is reversible airway narrowing and is usually discussed with it.)

- **Causes and risks**: smoking (main cause), indoor air pollution from biomass cooking fuels (important in India), occupational dust, outdoor pollution, repeated infections, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (rare).
- **Pathophysiology**:
  - Chronic bronchitis: irritants → more mucus glands and mucus, damaged cilia → airway narrowing and productive cough (cough with sputum for at least 3 months a year for 2 years in a row).
  - Emphysema: destruction of alveolar walls → large air spaces, loss of elastic recoil → air trapping, barrel chest.
  - Long-standing low oxygen → narrowing of lung vessels → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure (cor pulmonale).

| Feature | Chronic bronchitis ("blue bloater") | Emphysema ("pink puffer") |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cough and sputum | Marked | Little |
| Cyanosis, oedema | Common | Less |
| Breathlessness | Later | Early and marked; pursed-lip breathing |
| Body build | Often heavy | Thin, barrel chest |

These are classic descriptions; most patients have features of both.

- **Diagnostic tests**: spirometry (reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio after bronchodilator confirms airflow limitation), chest X-ray (hyperinflation), ABG, sputum culture, ECG and echo (cor pulmonale), CBC (polycythaemia).
- **Medical management (classes)**: bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists, anticholinergics), inhaled corticosteroids in some, mucolytics, antibiotics in infective attacks, **controlled oxygen** therapy, vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal), pulmonary rehabilitation. Severe disease: long-term oxygen therapy, non-invasive ventilation; surgery (bullectomy, lung volume reduction) in selected patients.
- **Important**: some COPD patients retain CO₂ and depend on low oxygen to drive breathing, so oxygen is given in the **controlled concentration ordered**, often by Venturi mask, aiming at the target saturation set by the doctor (commonly 88–92%), and the patient is watched for drowsiness.

**Nursing diagnoses and interventions**

| Diagnosis | Interventions (with rationale) |
| --- | --- |
| Ineffective airway clearance related to thick secretions | High-Fowler's or tripod position (lungs expand); fluids if not restricted (thin secretions); steam/nebulisation as ordered; controlled and huff coughing; chest physiotherapy and postural drainage; suction if needed |
| Impaired gas exchange related to airflow limitation | Controlled oxygen as ordered; monitor SpO₂, ABG, level of consciousness; pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing (keeps airways open, empties lungs) |
| Activity intolerance related to breathlessness | Plan rest between activities; graded exercise; energy-saving techniques |
| Imbalanced nutrition, less than body requirement | Small frequent high-calorie, high-protein meals; rest before meals; mouth care after inhalers |
| Anxiety related to breathlessness | Stay with the patient, calm voice, teach breathing control |

**Patient education**: stop smoking (most important); avoid smoke and dust, use cleaner cooking fuel and ventilation; correct inhaler and spacer technique; rinse mouth after steroid inhalers; recognise early signs of infection (change in sputum colour, more breathlessness); vaccination; breathing exercises; safe home oxygen use (no smoking or fire near oxygen).

### Bronchial asthma (brief)

- Chronic inflammation of airways with episodes of reversible narrowing (bronchospasm, oedema, mucus).
- Triggers: allergens (dust mite, pollen, animal dander), smoke, cold air, exercise, infection, some drugs.
- Features: episodes of wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, cough worse at night or early morning.
- Management (classes): relievers (short-acting beta-2 agonists), controllers (inhaled corticosteroids, long-acting beta-2 agonists), leukotriene modifiers.
- **Acute severe asthma**: high-Fowler's position, oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids as ordered; danger signs — cannot speak a sentence, silent chest, drowsiness, cyanosis.
- Teaching: avoid triggers, peak-flow monitoring, written action plan, inhaler technique.

## 3.5 Pleural effusion and empyema

**Pleural effusion**: abnormal collection of fluid in the pleural space.

- **Transudate** (low protein): heart failure, cirrhosis, kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome).
- **Exudate** (high protein): tuberculosis (common in India), pneumonia, cancer, pulmonary embolism.
- **Features**: breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, reduced chest movement on the affected side, **stony dull percussion**, reduced or absent breath sounds, trachea pushed to the opposite side in large effusions.
- **Tests**: chest X-ray (blunting of costophrenic angle), ultrasound, thoracentesis with fluid analysis.
- **Management**: treat the cause; thoracentesis; intercostal chest drain for large effusions; **pleurodesis** (sealing the pleural space with an agent) for recurrent effusions.

**Empyema**: pus in the pleural space, usually after pneumonia, lung abscess or chest surgery. Features: high fever, chills, chest pain, toxic look. Management: antibiotics, chest drain, and if the pus is thick or loculated, surgery (decortication).

### Care of a patient with an intercostal chest drain (underwater seal)

1. Keep the drainage bottle **below chest level** at all times. — *Prevents fluid flowing back into the chest.*
2. Keep the tube end under the water (about 2 cm). — *The water acts as a one-way seal so air cannot enter the chest.*
3. Check **tidaling** (water level rising and falling with breathing) — shows the tube is open; stopped tidaling may mean blockage or re-expanded lung.
4. **Bubbling**: continuous bubbling may mean an air leak in the system; intermittent bubbling on coughing is expected with pneumothorax.
5. Keep tubes free from kinks and loops; secure connections with tape.
6. Keep two clamps at the bedside, but **do not clamp routinely** (risk of tension pneumothorax); clamp only briefly when changing bottles or if the system disconnects, as per policy.
7. Record amount, colour and nature of drainage; report sudden increase (bleeding) or more than the limit set.
8. Encourage deep breathing, coughing and arm and shoulder exercises.
9. If the tube comes out of the chest, cover the site at once with a sterile dressing and inform the doctor.

## 3.6 Bronchiectasis

- **Definition**: permanent abnormal widening of bronchi with destruction of their walls.
- **Causes**: severe childhood infections (measles, whooping cough), tuberculosis, cystic fibrosis, obstruction by tumour or foreign body, immune defects.
- **Pathophysiology**: infection and inflammation damage the bronchial wall → bronchi widen → mucus pools → repeated infection (vicious circle).
- **Features**: chronic cough with **large amounts of foul-smelling purulent sputum**, especially in the morning and on changing position; haemoptysis; clubbing; coarse crackles.
- **Tests**: high-resolution CT (the test of choice), sputum culture, spirometry.
- **Management**: postural drainage and chest physiotherapy (main nursing measure), antibiotics during attacks, bronchodilators, mucolytics; surgical removal (lobectomy) for localised disease.
- **Nursing**: postural drainage two to three times a day before meals, sputum cup with lid and record of daily amount, good mouth care, high-protein diet, fluids, teach the family chest physiotherapy.

## 3.7 Pneumonia

- **Definition**: acute inflammation of lung tissue (alveoli) usually caused by infection, with filling of alveoli by exudate (consolidation).
- **Classification**: community-acquired, hospital-acquired (including ventilator-associated), aspiration pneumonia, pneumonia in immunocompromised patients; anatomically lobar or bronchopneumonia.
- **Organisms**: bacteria (commonly *Streptococcus pneumoniae*), viruses, fungi, atypical organisms.
- **Risk factors**: old age, smoking, alcohol, COPD, diabetes, immobility, reduced consciousness, poor swallowing, ventilation.
- **Pathophysiology (lobar)**: congestion → red hepatisation → grey hepatisation → resolution.
- **Features**: fever with chills, cough with rusty or purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, rapid breathing, crackles, bronchial breath sounds and dullness over consolidation; confusion in the elderly.
- **Tests**: chest X-ray, sputum Gram stain and culture, blood culture, CBC (raised white cells), ABG, SpO₂.
- **Management**: antibiotics as ordered (after cultures are sent), oxygen, fluids, antipyretics; ventilation in severe cases.

**Nursing care**: semi- or high-Fowler's position; oxygen; deep breathing, coughing, incentive spirometry; fluids 2–3 litres/day if not restricted; tepid sponging for fever; rest; mouth care; turning two-hourly; monitor temperature, respiration, SpO₂.

**Prevention of hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia**: hand hygiene, head end raised 30–45°, oral care, early mobilisation, aspiration precautions, aseptic suctioning.

## 3.8 Lung abscess

- Localised area of pus formation with destruction of lung tissue (cavity).
- Causes: aspiration (alcoholism, unconsciousness, poor dental hygiene), pneumonia, obstruction by a tumour.
- Features: fever, cough with large amounts of foul, sometimes blood-stained sputum, chest pain, weight loss, clubbing.
- Tests: chest X-ray and CT (cavity with air–fluid level), sputum culture.
- Management: long course of antibiotics, postural drainage; surgery (lobectomy) if not resolving.
- Nursing: as for bronchiectasis; good oral hygiene; nutrition.

## 3.9 Cysts and tumours of the lung

- **Lung cysts** (e.g. hydatid cyst from dog tapeworm, congenital cysts, bullae): may be silent or cause cough, pain, infection; surgical removal when needed.
- **Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma)**:
  - Risk factors: smoking (main), passive smoking, air pollution, occupational exposure (asbestos, radon).
  - Types: non-small-cell (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large cell) and small-cell.
  - Features: persistent cough, haemoptysis, chest pain, breathlessness, hoarseness, weight loss, recurrent pneumonia; signs of spread.
  - Tests: chest X-ray, CT, bronchoscopy with biopsy, sputum cytology, PET scan for staging.
  - Management: surgery (lobectomy, pneumonectomy), radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy; palliative care.

**After lung surgery**: chest drain care (no drain or drain as per surgeon after pneumonectomy); position as advised (after pneumonectomy usually on the back or partly turned towards the operated side, not on the unoperated side, so the remaining lung can expand — follow the surgeon's order); pain relief to allow deep breathing; arm exercises on the operated side; early ambulation.

## 3.10 Chest injuries

| Injury | Features | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Rib fracture** | Pain on breathing, tenderness | Pain relief to allow deep breathing; do not strap the chest |
| **Flail chest** (several ribs broken in two places) | **Paradoxical movement** — the segment moves in on inspiration | Oxygen, analgesia, ventilation in severe cases |
| **Pneumothorax** (air in pleural space) | Sudden chest pain, breathlessness, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds | Oxygen, needle aspiration or chest drain |
| **Tension pneumothorax** | Severe breathlessness, trachea shifted to opposite side, distended neck veins, low BP | Emergency needle decompression, then chest drain |
| **Open (sucking) chest wound** | Air sucked in through the wound | Cover with a dressing taped on three sides (acts as a flutter valve); chest drain |
| **Haemothorax** (blood in pleural space) | Dullness, shock | Chest drain, blood replacement; surgery if heavy bleeding |
| Cardiac tamponade | See Unit 5 | Pericardiocentesis |

First aid in chest injury: airway, breathing, circulation; oxygen; position upright if spine is not injured; cover open wounds; shift to hospital.

## 3.11 Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)

- **Definition**: sudden, severe inflammatory lung injury causing leaky capillaries, fluid-filled alveoli (non-cardiac pulmonary oedema) and severe hypoxaemia not corrected by ordinary oxygen.
- **Causes**: sepsis (commonest), pneumonia, aspiration, major trauma, shock, multiple transfusions, pancreatitis, drowning, burns.
- **Pathophysiology**: injury → inflammation → damaged alveolar–capillary membrane → protein-rich fluid floods alveoli → surfactant lost → alveoli collapse → stiff lungs → severe hypoxaemia → later fibrosis.
- **Features**: increasing breathlessness, rapid breathing, cyanosis, falling SpO₂ despite oxygen, crackles; chest X-ray shows "white-out" on both sides.
- **Management**: treat the cause; mechanical ventilation with lung-protective settings and PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) to keep alveoli open; prone positioning in severe cases; careful fluids; sedation.
- **Nursing**: ICU monitoring, ventilator care, suctioning, positioning, pressure-area care, nutrition, prevention of infection, family support.

## 3.12 Pulmonary embolism

- **Definition**: blockage of a pulmonary artery or its branch, usually by a blood clot that has travelled from a deep vein of the leg or pelvis.
- **Risk factors (Virchow's triad)**: slowing of blood flow (immobility, long journeys, surgery), damage to vessel wall (trauma, surgery), increased clotting (pregnancy, oral contraceptives, cancer, dehydration).
- **Features**: sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, rapid breathing and pulse, anxiety, cough, haemoptysis; large embolism → collapse, shock, death.
- **Tests**: CT pulmonary angiography (main test), D-dimer, ECG, ABG, ventilation-perfusion scan, leg Doppler ultrasound.
- **Management**: oxygen, anticoagulants as ordered, thrombolytics in massive embolism, rarely embolectomy; vena cava filter in selected cases.
- **Nursing**: high-Fowler's position, oxygen, monitoring; watch for bleeding during anticoagulant therapy (gums, urine, stools, injection sites); bleeding precautions (soft toothbrush, electric shaver).
- **Prevention**: early ambulation after surgery, leg exercises, graduated compression stockings and intermittent pneumatic compression as ordered, adequate fluids, preventive anticoagulants in high-risk patients as ordered.

## 3.13 Common respiratory nursing procedures

- **Oxygen therapy**: by nasal prongs (low flow), simple face mask, Venturi mask (fixed accurate concentration), non-rebreather mask (high concentration). Safety: no smoking or open flame, check humidifier, check skin under mask and prongs, give only the flow ordered, monitor SpO₂.
- **Nebulisation**: sitting position, slow deep breaths through mouthpiece or mask, mouth rinse after steroid nebulisation.
- **Chest physiotherapy**: percussion (cupped hands), vibration, postural drainage — before meals, not over spine, breasts or kidneys; stop if the patient becomes breathless or cyanosed.
- **Incentive spirometry**: slow deep breath held 3–5 seconds, 10 times an hour while awake.
- **Suctioning**: sterile technique for tracheal suction; pre-oxygenate; suction only while withdrawing; each pass no longer than about 10–15 seconds.

## 3.14 Health behaviours to prevent respiratory illness

- Do not smoke; avoid second-hand smoke; tobacco cessation help (quit lines and cessation centres).
- Use cleaner cooking fuel (LPG), smokeless stoves and good kitchen ventilation.
- Masks and protective equipment at dusty workplaces.
- Cover coughs and sneezes (respiratory hygiene), hand hygiene, masks during epidemics.
- Vaccinations as advised (influenza, pneumococcal, BCG in childhood).
- Early treatment of respiratory infections; complete the full course of TB treatment.
- Healthy diet, exercise, avoid overcrowding, good house ventilation.

## Remember

- Breath sounds: crackles = fluid in alveoli; wheeze = narrowed airways; stridor = upper airway obstruction (emergency).
- Stony dull percussion = pleural effusion; hyper-resonance = pneumothorax.
- Sputum: early morning, deep cough, sterile container, before antibiotics.
- COPD = chronic bronchitis + emphysema; smoking and biomass smoke; give oxygen only as ordered, controlled.
- Pursed-lip breathing keeps airways open.
- Chest drain bottle below the chest; do not clamp routinely; tidaling shows the tube is open.
- Bronchiectasis: large amounts of foul sputum; postural drainage.
- Flail chest = paradoxical movement; tension pneumothorax = trachea shift + distended neck veins + low BP.
- Open chest wound: dressing taped on three sides.
- ARDS: severe hypoxaemia not corrected by oxygen; ventilation with PEEP; prone position.
- Pulmonary embolism usually comes from a leg DVT; prevent with early ambulation.

# Unit 4: Nursing management of patients with disorders of the digestive system

This notes file covers INC Unit V (16 hours): GI assessment and investigations, disorders of the mouth, stomach, intestines, anus, pancreas, liver and gall bladder, and the GI procedures you must perform — gastric decompression, gavage (tube feeding), stoma care and feeding techniques. Drugs are named by class only.

## 4.1 Review of anatomy and physiology

```text
 Mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → jejunum → ileum
       → caecum (appendix) → ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid colon
       → rectum → anal canal
 Accessory organs: salivary glands, liver, gall bladder, pancreas
```

- **Stomach**: stores food, secretes hydrochloric acid, pepsin and intrinsic factor (needed for vitamin B12 absorption).
- **Small intestine**: main site of digestion and absorption (villi).
- **Large intestine**: absorbs water and electrolytes, forms faeces.
- **Liver**: makes bile, proteins (albumin, clotting factors), stores glycogen, detoxifies drugs and ammonia.
- **Pancreas**: exocrine enzymes (amylase, lipase, trypsin) and endocrine hormones (insulin, glucagon).

## 4.2 Nursing assessment

### History

Appetite, weight change, difficulty in swallowing (dysphagia), pain on swallowing, nausea and vomiting (amount, colour — coffee-ground means altered blood), heartburn, abdominal pain (site, type, relation to food), bowel habits, diarrhoea, constipation, blood in stools (fresh red or black tarry = melaena), jaundice, alcohol intake, diet, past surgery, medicines (NSAIDs, steroids).

### Physical assessment of the abdomen

Order for the abdomen is **inspection → auscultation → percussion → palpation** — auscultation comes before palpation because touching changes bowel sounds.

| Step | Look for |
| --- | --- |
| Inspection | Shape (flat, distended), scars, visible peristalsis, dilated veins (caput medusae), hernias, jaundice of skin and eyes |
| Auscultation | Bowel sounds normally about 5–30 per minute; absent (paralytic ileus, peritonitis), high-pitched tinkling (obstruction) |
| Percussion | Tympany (gas), dullness (fluid, organs, masses); shifting dullness in ascites; liver span |
| Palpation | Tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness, masses, enlarged liver or spleen |

Also examine the mouth, and the perianal area when indicated.

### Nine regions of the abdomen

```text
 Right hypochondrium | Epigastrium | Left hypochondrium
 Right lumbar        | Umbilical   | Left lumbar
 Right iliac (inguinal)| Hypogastrium (suprapubic) | Left iliac
```

## 4.3 GI investigations and nursing preparation

| Investigation | Preparation and after-care |
| --- | --- |
| **Upper GI endoscopy** (oesophagogastroduodenoscopy) | Nil by mouth before as ordered; remove dentures; throat spray; after: nil by mouth until gag reflex returns; watch for pain, bleeding, fever (perforation) |
| **Colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy** | Clear liquid diet the day before; bowel preparation as ordered; after: watch for bleeding, abdominal pain; passing gas is normal |
| **Barium swallow / meal** | Nil by mouth before; after: fluids and laxative as ordered; stools will be white for a few days |
| **Barium enema** | Bowel preparation; after: fluids, laxative |
| Ultrasound abdomen | Nil by mouth for gall bladder studies; full bladder for pelvic scan |
| CT, MRI | Ask about contrast allergy and kidney function |
| **Liver function tests** | Bilirubin, liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP), albumin, prothrombin time |
| **Stool examination** | Occult blood, ova and cysts, culture; fresh sample |
| ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) | As for endoscopy; watch for pancreatitis after |
| **Liver biopsy** | Check clotting tests and platelets; after: lie on the **right side** for a few hours (pressure on the site), monitor pulse and BP for bleeding |
| **Paracentesis** (abdominal tap) | Empty the bladder (avoid puncture); sitting position; record weight and girth before and after; watch BP |

## 4.4 Disorders of the oral cavity — lips, gums and teeth

| Condition | Features | Care |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Stomatitis** (inflammation of mouth) | Painful ulcers; causes: infection, vitamin deficiency, chemotherapy | Soft bland food, mouth care with mild solutions, avoid spicy food |
| **Oral candidiasis (thrush)** | White patches that leave a raw area when scraped | Antifungal agents; denture hygiene |
| **Aphthous ulcer** | Painful shallow ulcers | Topical agents; avoid irritants |
| **Gingivitis, periodontitis** | Bleeding, swollen gums; tooth loss later | Brushing, flossing, dental care |
| **Dental caries** | Decay of teeth | Reduce sugar, fluoride toothpaste, dental visits |
| **Cleft lip/palate** (in adults: after repair) | Feeding and speech problems | Surgery and speech therapy |
| **Oral cancer** | Non-healing ulcer, white (leukoplakia) or red patches, lump; risk: tobacco chewing, smoking, betel quid, alcohol — a major cancer in India | Biopsy; surgery, radiotherapy; tobacco cessation, early screening |

## 4.5 GI bleeding

- **Upper GI bleeding** (above the ligament of Treitz): peptic ulcer, oesophageal varices, gastritis, Mallory-Weiss tear, cancer. Presents as **haematemesis** (vomiting blood) and **melaena** (black tarry stools).
- **Lower GI bleeding**: haemorrhoids, fissure, colon cancer, diverticular disease, inflammatory bowel disease. Presents as fresh red blood per rectum (haematochezia).
- **Management**: airway, two large IV lines, fluids and blood as ordered, nil by mouth, monitor pulse, BP and urine output, nasogastric tube if ordered, endoscopy to find and stop the bleed; acid-reducing drugs (proton pump inhibitors) as ordered; surgery if bleeding continues.
- **Nursing**: lie flat with legs raised if in shock; side position if vomiting; record amount and colour of blood loss; reassure; mouth care.

## 4.6 Infections and inflammation of the GI tract

- **Gastritis**: inflammation of the stomach lining — acute (alcohol, NSAIDs, food poisoning, stress) or chronic (*Helicobacter pylori*, autoimmune). Features: epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, indigestion. Care: remove the cause, small bland meals, acid-reducing drugs as ordered.
- **Gastroenteritis**: infection causing vomiting and diarrhoea (viral, bacterial, parasitic). Main risk is dehydration. Care: oral rehydration solution, IV fluids if severe, hygiene (see Unit 9 on diarrhoeal diseases).
- **Inflammatory bowel disease**:

| Feature | Ulcerative colitis | Crohn's disease |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Site | Rectum and colon only, continuous | Any part from mouth to anus, mostly terminal ileum; skip areas |
| Depth | Mucosa only | Full thickness of the wall |
| Main symptom | Bloody diarrhoea with mucus | Abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss |
| Complications | Toxic megacolon, colon cancer | Strictures, fistulas, abscesses |
| Surgery | Removal of colon can cure | Not curative; done for complications |

Management (classes): anti-inflammatory agents (aminosalicylates), corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, biological agents; nutritional support; surgery (colectomy with ileostomy) when needed. Nursing: record stool frequency and character, fluids and electrolytes, perianal skin care, nutrition, emotional support.

## 4.7 Peptic and duodenal ulcer

- **Definition**: an erosion of the mucosa in areas exposed to acid and pepsin — stomach (gastric ulcer) or duodenum (duodenal ulcer, the commoner).
- **Causes**: *Helicobacter pylori* infection (main), NSAIDs, smoking, alcohol, stress, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (rare).
- **Pathophysiology**: imbalance between attacking factors (acid, pepsin, *H. pylori*, NSAIDs) and protective factors (mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow, prostaglandins) → mucosa erodes.

| Point | Gastric ulcer | Duodenal ulcer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pain | Soon after meals | 2–3 hours after meals and at night; relieved by food |
| Weight | May lose weight (fear of eating) | Often normal or gain |
| Acid level | Normal or low | High |
| Cancer risk | Possible — biopsy needed | Very rare |

- **Tests**: upper GI endoscopy with biopsy; tests for *H. pylori* (urea breath test, stool antigen, biopsy); stool occult blood; CBC (anaemia).
- **Medical management (classes)**: proton pump inhibitors, H2-receptor blockers, antacids, mucosal protective agents; *H. pylori* eradication therapy (combination of a proton pump inhibitor with antibiotics); stop NSAIDs, smoking and alcohol.
- **Complications**: bleeding, **perforation** (sudden severe pain, board-like rigid abdomen, shock — surgical emergency), gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis — projectile vomiting of old food), malignancy (gastric).
- **Surgical management** (now less common): oversewing a perforation; vagotomy with pyloroplasty; partial gastrectomy (Billroth I, II).
- **After gastric surgery — dumping syndrome**: food passes quickly into the jejunum → faintness, sweating, palpitation, cramps, diarrhoea soon after meals. Teach small frequent dry meals, fluids between meals rather than with meals, more protein and fat, less simple sugar, lie down after meals.

**Nursing care**: regular small meals, avoid foods that cause pain, stop smoking and alcohol, avoid NSAIDs, take drugs as ordered and complete the eradication course, stress reduction, report black stools or vomiting blood.

## 4.8 Tumours of the GI tract

- **Oesophageal cancer**: progressive dysphagia (first solids, then liquids), weight loss; risk: tobacco, alcohol, hot drinks, achalasia, Barrett's oesophagus.
- **Gastric cancer**: indigestion, early fullness, weight loss, anaemia, mass, vomiting; risk: *H. pylori*, smoked and salted foods.
- **Colorectal cancer**: change in bowel habit, blood in stools, tenesmus, anaemia, weight loss, obstruction; risk: age, low-fibre high-fat diet, inflammatory bowel disease, polyps, family history.
- Tests: endoscopy and biopsy, CT, tumour markers (e.g. CEA for colorectal cancer, used for follow-up).
- Management: surgery (oesophagectomy, gastrectomy, hemicolectomy, abdominoperineal resection with colostomy), chemotherapy, radiotherapy, palliative care; nutritional support.

## 4.9 Intestinal obstruction

- **Definition**: blockage of the forward flow of intestinal contents.
- **Types**:
  - **Mechanical**: adhesions (commonest after surgery), hernia, tumour, volvulus (twisting), intussusception, faecal impaction, strictures.
  - **Non-mechanical (paralytic ileus)**: loss of peristalsis after abdominal surgery, peritonitis, hypokalaemia, spinal injury.
- **Pathophysiology**: blockage → gas and fluid collect above it → distension → vomiting and fluid loss → dehydration and electrolyte loss → pressure on bowel wall → reduced blood supply → strangulation, gangrene, perforation, peritonitis, shock.
- **Features**: colicky abdominal pain, vomiting (early and bilious in small-bowel obstruction; late and faeculent in large-bowel obstruction), distension, constipation with no gas passed (absolute constipation), high-pitched bowel sounds (silent in ileus).
- **Tests**: abdominal X-ray (dilated loops, fluid levels), CT, electrolytes.
- **Management**: "drip and suck" — nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and electrolytes; surgery for strangulation or if not resolving (adhesiolysis, resection, colostomy).
- **Nursing**: nasogastric tube care, intake and output, monitor girth, vital signs, mouth care, pain assessment, prepare for surgery.

## 4.10 Perforation and peritonitis

- **Peritonitis**: inflammation of the peritoneum, usually from perforation of a hollow organ (ulcer, appendix, bowel, typhoid perforation of ileum) or infection.
- **Features**: severe abdominal pain worse on movement, patient lies still, **board-like rigidity**, rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds, fever, rapid pulse, vomiting, shock.
- **Tests**: erect chest X-ray (gas under the diaphragm in perforation), CBC, CT.
- **Management**: nil by mouth, nasogastric suction, IV fluids, antibiotics, analgesia as ordered; emergency surgery (laparotomy, closure of perforation, peritoneal lavage).
- **Nursing**: semi-Fowler's position (pus collects in the pelvis rather than under the diaphragm), monitor vital signs and urine output, care of drains and wound.

## 4.11 Malabsorption

- Failure to absorb nutrients from the small intestine.
- Causes: coeliac disease (gluten intolerance), lactose intolerance, tropical sprue, chronic pancreatitis, short bowel after resection, Crohn's disease.
- Features: diarrhoea, bulky pale foul-smelling floating stools (steatorrhoea), weight loss, anaemia, vitamin and mineral deficiencies, oedema.
- Management: treat the cause — gluten-free diet in coeliac disease (avoid wheat, barley, rye), lactose-free diet, pancreatic enzyme replacement, vitamin and mineral supplements.

## 4.12 Appendicitis

- **Definition**: inflammation of the vermiform appendix, usually from blockage of its opening (faecolith, lymphoid swelling).
- **Features**: pain starts around the umbilicus and **shifts to the right iliac fossa**; tenderness at **McBurney's point** (one-third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus); rebound tenderness; low-grade fever, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite. Rovsing's sign: pressing on the left iliac fossa causes pain on the right.
- **Tests**: CBC (raised white cells), ultrasound, CT.
- **Management**: appendicectomy (open or laparoscopic); antibiotics.
- **Nursing before surgery**: nil by mouth, IV fluids, **no laxatives, no enema and no heat pad on the abdomen** (they can cause rupture), pain relief as ordered.
- **Complications**: perforation → peritonitis; appendicular mass or abscess.

## 4.13 Hernias

- **Definition**: protrusion of an organ or tissue through a weak area in the wall that normally contains it.
- **Types**: inguinal (indirect and direct — commonest in men), femoral (more in women), umbilical, paraumbilical, incisional (through an old scar), hiatus hernia (stomach through the diaphragm).
- **States**: reducible, irreducible (incarcerated), **obstructed**, **strangulated** (blood supply cut off — painful, tender, red, emergency).
- **Management**: hernia repair — herniorrhaphy, hernioplasty with mesh (open or laparoscopic).
- **After repair**: avoid straining, coughing with support of the wound, prevent constipation, no heavy lifting for the period advised (often several weeks), scrotal support and ice packs if there is scrotal swelling after inguinal repair.

## 4.14 Haemorrhoids, fissures and fistulas

| Condition | Features | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Haemorrhoids (piles)** — dilated veins of the anal canal; internal (above dentate line) or external | Painless bright red bleeding with stools (internal), prolapse, itching; painful if thrombosed (external) | High-fibre diet, fluids, sitz baths, stool softeners; rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy; haemorrhoidectomy, stapler surgery |
| **Anal fissure** — tear in the lining of the anal canal | Severe pain during and after defecation, small amount of bright blood | Fibre, fluids, sitz baths, topical agents; lateral sphincterotomy if chronic |
| **Fistula-in-ano** — abnormal track from anal canal to perianal skin, usually after an abscess | Discharge of pus, recurrent abscesses | Fistulotomy, seton, other procedures |

**After anorectal surgery**: pain relief, **sitz bath** two to three times a day and after each bowel movement (cleans and relieves spasm), stool softeners, high-fibre diet and fluids so the first motion is soft, watch for bleeding and urinary retention.

## 4.15 Disorders of the pancreas

### Acute pancreatitis

- **Definition**: acute inflammation of the pancreas in which enzymes become active inside the gland and digest it (autodigestion).
- **Causes**: gallstones and alcohol (commonest), high triglycerides, trauma, ERCP, some drugs, mumps.
- **Features**: sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, relieved partly by sitting and leaning forward; nausea, vomiting; fever; tachycardia; shock in severe cases; bruising in the flanks (Grey Turner's sign) or around the umbilicus (Cullen's sign) in severe haemorrhagic cases.
- **Tests**: serum amylase and lipase (raised; lipase more specific), ultrasound (gallstones), CT, calcium (low in severe disease), blood sugar.
- **Management**: nil by mouth initially, IV fluids (very important), analgesics as ordered, nasogastric suction if vomiting, early enteral feeding as ordered, treat the cause (ERCP for stones, later cholecystectomy), ICU care if severe; surgery for infected necrosis.
- **Nursing**: pain relief, position of comfort (sitting forward, knees flexed), fluid balance, monitor blood sugar and calcium (watch for tetany), breathing (risk of ARDS), no alcohol.

### Chronic pancreatitis

Repeated inflammation → fibrosis and loss of function. Mostly alcohol. Features: recurrent pain, steatorrhoea, weight loss, diabetes. Management: no alcohol, pain relief, pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals, low-fat diet, diabetes care.

### Pancreatic cysts and tumours

- **Pseudocyst**: fluid collection after pancreatitis; drained if large or symptomatic.
- **Carcinoma of the pancreas**: painless progressive jaundice (head of pancreas), weight loss, back pain, new diabetes; poor outlook. Whipple's operation (pancreaticoduodenectomy) when possible; palliative stenting of the bile duct.

## 4.16 Disorders of the liver

### Hepatitis (inflammation of the liver)

Viral hepatitis A to E is covered in Unit 9. Other causes: alcohol, drugs, autoimmune. Features: fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, tender liver.

### Liver abscess

- **Amoebic** (from *Entamoeba histolytica*; common in India) or **pyogenic** (bacterial).
- Features: fever, pain in the right upper abdomen, tender enlarged liver.
- Management: drugs against amoeba or antibiotics as ordered; aspiration or drainage for large abscesses.

### Liver cysts

Simple cysts (usually harmless) and **hydatid cyst** (dog tapeworm — anti-parasitic drugs and surgery; rupture can cause anaphylaxis).

### Cirrhosis of the liver

- **Definition**: chronic, irreversible liver disease in which normal tissue is replaced by fibrous scar and regenerating nodules, distorting liver structure and function.
- **Causes**: alcohol, chronic hepatitis B and C, fatty liver disease (obesity, diabetes), biliary obstruction, autoimmune and inherited disorders.
- **Pathophysiology**: repeated cell death → fibrosis and nodules → (1) loss of liver cell function and (2) obstructed blood flow through the liver → **portal hypertension**.

| Result of liver cell failure | Result of portal hypertension |
| --- | --- |
| Jaundice | Oesophageal varices (can bleed) |
| Low albumin → oedema and ascites | Splenomegaly (low platelets) |
| Low clotting factors → bleeding | Ascites |
| Raised ammonia → hepatic encephalopathy | Caput medusae, haemorrhoids |
| Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia | |

- **Tests**: liver function tests, prothrombin time/INR, CBC (low platelets), ultrasound, endoscopy (varices), viral markers, liver biopsy or elastography.
- **Management**: stop alcohol; treat the cause (antiviral drugs for hepatitis B or C); diet; diuretics, salt restriction and paracentesis for ascites; beta-blockers and endoscopic band ligation for varices; lactulose and gut antibiotics for encephalopathy; liver transplantation for end-stage disease.

**Nursing diagnoses and care**

| Diagnosis | Interventions |
| --- | --- |
| Excess fluid volume (ascites, oedema) | Salt restriction (and fluid restriction if ordered), daily weight and abdominal girth, intake and output, semi-Fowler's position for breathing |
| Imbalanced nutrition | Small frequent meals, adequate calories; normal protein intake is generally advised, with limits only as ordered during acute encephalopathy; vitamins |
| Risk for bleeding | Watch gums, stools and vomit; soft toothbrush; avoid injections where possible; pressure after needle pricks |
| Risk for injury (confusion) | Watch for drowsiness, confusion, flapping tremor (asterixis); prevent constipation (lactulose as ordered); safety measures |
| Impaired skin integrity (itching, oedema) | Cool baths, mild soap, keep nails short, turn frequently |

### Portal hypertension and bleeding varices

Raised pressure in the portal vein → collateral veins swell, especially at the lower oesophagus. Variceal bleeding causes massive haematemesis. Emergency care: airway, IV lines, blood, drugs to reduce portal pressure (vasoconstrictors) as ordered, emergency endoscopic band ligation or sclerotherapy; balloon tamponade tube (e.g. Sengstaken-Blakemore) temporarily — keep scissors at the bedside to cut and remove it if it slips up and blocks the airway; TIPS (shunt) in selected patients.

### Hepatic failure (liver failure)

- Acute (e.g. viral hepatitis, drug overdose such as paracetamol overdose) or chronic (end-stage cirrhosis).
- Features: jaundice, bleeding, encephalopathy (stages from confusion to coma), kidney failure (hepatorenal syndrome), low blood sugar.
- Care: ICU, airway, blood sugar monitoring, measures to lower ammonia, avoid sedatives, transplantation.

### Liver tumours

Hepatocellular carcinoma (often on cirrhosis, hepatitis B and C), and secondaries from other organs (commoner). Features: weight loss, pain, mass, worsening liver function. Tests: alpha-fetoprotein, imaging, biopsy. Management: surgery, local ablation, chemoembolisation, targeted drugs, transplantation, palliation. Prevention: hepatitis B vaccination.

## 4.17 Disorders of the gall bladder

### Cholelithiasis and cholecystitis

- **Cholelithiasis**: stones in the gall bladder (cholesterol, pigment or mixed). Risk factors ("5 F": female, fat, fertile, forty, fair — a memory aid only), rapid weight loss, family history.
- **Cholecystitis**: inflammation of the gall bladder, usually from a stone blocking the cystic duct.
- **Features**: biliary colic — severe pain in the right upper abdomen or epigastrium, often after a fatty meal, radiating to the right shoulder or back; nausea, vomiting; fever and **Murphy's sign** (pain and catch in breathing when pressing under the right ribs) in cholecystitis; jaundice if a stone blocks the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis).
- **Tests**: ultrasound (test of choice), liver function tests, CBC, MRCP or ERCP for duct stones.
- **Management**: pain relief, antibiotics, IV fluids; **laparoscopic cholecystectomy** (standard treatment); ERCP to remove duct stones.
- **After cholecystectomy**: early ambulation; shoulder-tip pain after laparoscopy (gas) settles; if a T-tube is placed after open duct exploration: keep the bag below the wound, record the amount of bile, protect the skin; low-fat diet initially if advised.

### Tumours of the gall bladder

Carcinoma of the gall bladder (more common in parts of North and North-East India) — often found late with pain, mass, jaundice; surgery if early, otherwise palliation.

## 4.18 Gastric decompression, gavage, stoma care and feeding techniques

### Nasogastric (NG) tube insertion — steps with rationale

1. Check the order; explain; sit the patient upright (high-Fowler's) with head slightly flexed. — *Eases passage into the oesophagus, not the trachea.*
2. Measure the length: **tip of the nose → earlobe → xiphisternum (NEX)** and mark it. — *Places the tip in the stomach.*
3. Lubricate the tip with water-soluble jelly. — *Reduces trauma; a water-soluble gel is safe if aspirated.*
4. Insert through the more open nostril, aiming backwards along the floor of the nose; ask the patient to swallow (sips of water if allowed) as the tube passes the throat. — *Swallowing closes the airway.*
5. Stop and withdraw if the patient coughs, chokes or becomes cyanosed. — *The tube may be in the airway.*
6. Check position: aspirate gastric contents and **test with pH paper (gastric pH is usually 5.5 or below)**; X-ray confirmation when in doubt or for fine-bore tubes. Auscultating air ("whoosh test") alone is not reliable. — *Prevents feeding into the lungs.*
7. Secure with tape to the nose; record length, position check, and the patient's response.

**Gastric decompression**: the NG tube is connected to free drainage or intermittent low suction to remove gas and fluid (intestinal obstruction, ileus, after GI surgery). Nursing: keep the tube patent (irrigate with saline only if ordered), record drainage amount and colour, replace fluid and electrolytes as ordered, mouth and nostril care, watch for electrolyte imbalance.

### Gavage (tube feeding)

1. Check tube position before every feed and every medicine. — *Prevents aspiration.*
2. Patient sitting up at least 30–45° during feed and for 30–60 minutes after. — *Reduces regurgitation and aspiration.*
3. Check gastric residual volume if the hospital policy requires it.
4. Flush with water before and after the feed and medicines. — *Keeps the tube open.*
5. Give feed at room temperature, slowly by gravity or pump; never force. — *Prevents cramps, diarrhoea and vomiting.*
6. Close the tube after the feed; record amount and tolerance.

**Feeding techniques**: oral feeding with help; nasogastric and nasojejunal feeding; gastrostomy (PEG — through the abdominal wall) and jejunostomy for long-term feeding; bolus, intermittent or continuous feeds; **total parenteral nutrition (TPN)** through a central venous line when the gut cannot be used — strict asepsis, monitor blood sugar, weight and electrolytes, never stop suddenly without an order.

### Stoma care (colostomy, ileostomy)

| Point | Colostomy | Ileostomy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Site | Large bowel | End of ileum |
| Output | Formed or semi-formed stool (more formed further along the colon) | Liquid, continuous, contains enzymes — irritates skin |
| Risks | Constipation | Dehydration, electrolyte loss, skin damage |

**Assess the stoma**: normal is moist, beefy red or pink, slightly raised. Dark red, purple or black means poor blood supply — report at once. Watch for retraction, prolapse, swelling and skin breakdown.

**Changing the pouch (steps)**

1. Explain; give privacy; encourage the patient to watch and take part. — *Promotes self-care and acceptance.*
2. Remove the old pouch gently, pushing the skin away from the wafer. — *Protects the skin.*
3. Clean the stoma and skin with warm water; pat dry. — *Soap residue can stop the wafer sticking.*
4. Measure the stoma; cut the wafer opening just slightly larger than the stoma (about 2–3 mm). — *Too large exposes skin to output; too small cuts the stoma.*
5. Apply skin barrier if needed; fit the wafer and pouch; hold for a minute (warmth helps adhesion).
6. Empty the pouch when about one-third to one-half full. — *Prevents leakage and the weight pulling it off.*
7. Record stoma appearance, output and skin condition.

**Patient teaching**: diet (avoid gas-forming foods if troublesome; ileostomy patients need plenty of fluids and salt), clothing, bathing, return to work, sexual concerns, support groups (ostomy associations), and when to seek help.

## 4.19 Drugs and alternative therapies in digestive disorders

| Drug class | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| Antacids, H2-receptor blockers, proton pump inhibitors | Acid disorders, ulcers, bleeding |
| Antiemetics | Nausea, vomiting |
| Laxatives and stool softeners | Constipation, before investigations, after anorectal surgery |
| Antidiarrhoeals, oral rehydration solution | Diarrhoea |
| Antispasmodics | Colicky pain |
| Antibiotics, anti-amoebic agents | Infections, *H. pylori*, abscesses |
| Aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants | Inflammatory bowel disease |
| Pancreatic enzymes | Pancreatic insufficiency |
| Diuretics, lactulose | Ascites, hepatic encephalopathy |

**Alternative therapies**: dietary approaches, yoga and relaxation for functional bowel symptoms, probiotics (curd), herbal remedies — always ask about herbs because some are harmful to the liver.

## Remember

- Abdomen: inspect → auscultate → percuss → palpate.
- Haematemesis and melaena = upper GI bleed.
- Duodenal ulcer pain is relieved by food and wakes the patient at night; *H. pylori* is the main cause.
- Perforation: sudden severe pain, board-like rigidity, gas under the diaphragm on erect X-ray.
- Intestinal obstruction: colicky pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation; "drip and suck".
- Appendicitis: McBurney's point; no enema, laxative or heat pad.
- Strangulated hernia is a surgical emergency.
- Acute pancreatitis: pain to the back, raised lipase and amylase; gallstones and alcohol.
- Cirrhosis → portal hypertension → varices, ascites, splenomegaly; watch for encephalopathy.
- Liver biopsy: lie on the right side after.
- Gallstones: ultrasound; laparoscopic cholecystectomy; Murphy's sign.
- NG tube length = nose → earlobe → xiphisternum; confirm position by pH test of aspirate.
- Healthy stoma is moist and red; dark or black stoma — report at once.
- Ileostomy output is liquid — watch fluids, electrolytes and skin.

# Unit 5: Nursing management of patients with cardiovascular problems (with BLS/BCLS)

This notes file covers INC Unit VI (cardiovascular disorders, 20 hours theory and 5 hours lab, including the Basic/Basic Cardiac Life Support module). It is the heaviest unit of the course, so plan two or three study sessions. Learn assessment first, then vascular disorders, then diseases of the heart itself, then rhythm problems and failure, and finish with cardiac arrest and life support.

## 5.1 Review of anatomy and physiology of the cardiovascular system

- The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump in the middle of the chest (mediastinum), apex pointing down and to the left at about the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line.
- Layers: pericardium (outer sac), myocardium (muscle), endocardium (inner lining). The pericardial sac holds a little fluid that lets the heart move without friction.
- Chambers and valves: right atrium and right ventricle (tricuspid valve between them, pulmonary valve to the lungs); left atrium and left ventricle (mitral valve between them, aortic valve to the body).
- Blood flow: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs (pick up oxygen) → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.
- The heart's own blood comes from the right and left coronary arteries, which arise from the aorta. Blockage here causes angina and heart attack.
- Conduction system (the heart's wiring) makes it beat on its own:

```text
SA node (pacemaker, right atrium) → AV node → bundle of His
   → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricles contract
```

- **Cardiac output** = heart rate × stroke volume (the blood pumped per beat). It depends on preload (filling), afterload (resistance the heart pumps against) and contractility (strength of the beat).
- **Blood pressure** = cardiac output × resistance in the vessels. It is controlled by the heart, the vessels, the kidneys and hormones.

## 5.2 Nursing assessment

**History**: chest pain (site, type, radiation, triggers, relief), breathlessness (on effort, lying flat — orthopnoea, waking at night — paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea), palpitations, swelling of feet, fainting, tiredness, cough; risk factors (smoking, high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity, family history, stress, lack of exercise); past rheumatic fever; current medicines.

**Physical assessment**: general look (distress, cyanosis, pallor), pulse (rate, rhythm, volume, equality in both arms), blood pressure (both arms, lying and standing), neck veins (raised in heart failure), oedema of feet and sacrum, apex beat, heart sounds (normal S1 and S2; added S3, S4, murmurs), lung bases (crackles in failure), peripheral pulses and capillary refill, weight.

```text
Chest pain of cardiac origin — classic pattern:
 Central/left chest, crushing or heavy, may spread to left arm, jaw or back,
 with sweating, nausea and breathlessness; brought on by effort or stress.
```

## 5.3 Invasive and non-invasive cardiac procedures

| Procedure | What it is | Nursing points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ECG (electrocardiogram)** | Records the heart's electrical activity; non-invasive | Clean dry skin, correct lead placement, patient relaxed and still |
| **Echocardiography** | Ultrasound of the heart; shows chambers, valves, pumping | No preparation; explain it is painless |
| **Stress test (TMT)** | ECG during exercise on a treadmill | Light meal, comfortable shoes; stop if chest pain or arrhythmia |
| **Chest X-ray** | Heart size, lung congestion | Remove metal objects |
| **Cardiac catheterisation / angiography** | A catheter passed from the groin or wrist to the coronary arteries, with dye | **Before**: consent, nil by mouth, check kidney function and allergy to contrast, mark peripheral pulses, shave/clean site. **After**: bed rest with the limb straight, pressure over the site, watch for bleeding and haematoma, check distal pulse, colour and warmth, encourage fluids to flush the dye |
| **Angioplasty (PTCA) and stenting** | The blocked artery is widened with a balloon and a stent | As for catheterisation; continue antiplatelet drugs as ordered |
| **Blood tests** | Cardiac markers (troponin, CK-MB) after chest pain; lipid profile; electrolytes | Correct timing of troponin samples |

## 5.4 Disorders of the vascular system

### Hypertension (high blood pressure)

- Persistently raised blood pressure. It is called the "silent killer" because it often has no symptoms until it damages organs.
- **Primary (essential)**: no single cause; linked to age, salt, obesity, stress, family history, alcohol, smoking. **Secondary**: due to another disease (kidney disease, endocrine disorders, pregnancy, some drugs).
- Effects if untreated: stroke, heart attack, heart failure, kidney failure, eye damage.
- Features when present: headache, dizziness, nose bleeds, blurred vision.
- Management: lifestyle change (less salt, weight loss, exercise, no smoking, less alcohol, stress control) and antihypertensive drugs (by class: diuretics, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers), taken regularly for life.
- Nursing: measure BP correctly (rested, correct cuff, both arms), teach the patient to take drugs daily even when feeling well, teach home monitoring, diet counselling, report very high readings and warning signs.

### Arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis

- **Arteriosclerosis**: thickening and hardening of artery walls with age.
- **Atherosclerosis**: fatty plaques (cholesterol) build up inside arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow; the main cause of coronary and peripheral artery disease.
- Risk factors: high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, high BP, obesity, inactivity.

### Raynaud's disease

- Sudden narrowing of small arteries of the fingers and toes, usually brought on by cold or stress; the fingers turn white, then blue, then red, with pain and numbness.
- Nursing: keep hands and body warm, avoid cold and smoking, protect fingers from injury.

### Aneurysm

- A weak, bulging part of an artery wall (commonly the aorta). Danger is rupture with severe bleeding.
- Features: a pulsating swelling, pain; sudden tearing pain and shock if it ruptures.
- Management: control blood pressure; surgical repair or stent graft for large aneurysms.
- Nursing: avoid straining, monitor BP and pulses, watch for signs of rupture (sudden pain, falling BP) — an emergency.

### Peripheral vascular (arterial and venous) disorders

- **Peripheral arterial disease**: narrowed leg arteries → pain in the calf on walking that eases with rest (intermittent claudication), cold pale foot, weak pulses, poor healing, gangrene. Nursing: keep legs slightly dependent, foot care, no smoking, graded walking, protect from injury.
- **Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)**: clot in a deep leg vein → calf pain, swelling, warmth, redness. Risk after surgery and long bed rest. Prevention: early movement, leg exercises, anti-embolism stockings, hydration. Danger: the clot can travel to the lung (pulmonary embolism). Do not massage the leg.
- **Varicose veins**: dilated twisted superficial veins, aching, swelling. Nursing: elevate legs, support stockings, avoid long standing.

## 5.5 Coronary artery disease

Coronary atherosclerosis narrows the coronary arteries so the heart muscle gets too little oxygen.

### Angina pectoris

- Chest pain from a temporary shortage of blood to the heart muscle, usually during effort or stress; it is relieved by rest and by nitroglycerine under the tongue.
- Pain is central or left, pressing, may spread to the arm or jaw, lasts a few minutes.
- Nursing during an attack: stop activity, sit the patient up, give oxygen and nitroglycerine as ordered, reassure, record. Teach the patient to avoid triggers and to carry the medicine.

### Myocardial infarction (heart attack)

- Death of part of the heart muscle because a coronary artery is completely blocked.
- Features: severe crushing central chest pain lasting more than 20–30 minutes, **not relieved by rest or nitroglycerine**, sweating, nausea, breathlessness, fear; sometimes silent in older people and diabetics.
- Diagnosis: ECG changes, raised cardiac markers (troponin), history.
- Immediate management (remember **MONA**, as ordered): Morphine for pain, Oxygen, Nitroglycerine, Aspirin (chewed); plus drugs to dissolve the clot (thrombolytics) or urgent angioplasty to open the artery; bed rest, continuous ECG monitoring.
- Nursing: relieve pain, complete rest to reduce the heart's work, continuous monitoring for arrhythmias, oxygen, calm reassurance, watch for complications (arrhythmia, heart failure, shock), gradual return to activity (cardiac rehabilitation), health teaching on diet, smoking, exercise and drugs.

## 5.6 Valvular disorders

- Valves may be **narrowed (stenosis)** so blood cannot pass easily, or **leaky (regurgitation/incompetence)** so blood flows backward.
- **Congenital**: present at birth. **Acquired**: most often from rheumatic heart disease; also from infection or ageing.
- Common lesions: mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation.
- Features: breathlessness, tiredness, palpitations, a murmur heard on listening, and later heart failure.
- Management: drugs for symptoms and heart failure, prevention of infective endocarditis, valve repair or replacement surgery.
- Nursing: activity as tolerated, monitor for failure, teach about drugs and the need to tell dentists and surgeons about the valve problem.

## 5.7 Rheumatic heart disease and inflammation of the heart

- **Rheumatic fever** follows a throat infection with group A streptococcus; the body's own defence damages the heart valves. **Rheumatic heart disease** is the lasting valve damage. It is prevented by treating sore throats properly and by long-term penicillin prophylaxis as ordered.
- **Pericarditis**: inflammation of the pericardium → sharp chest pain that is worse on lying down and on deep breathing, a rubbing sound on listening, fever. Danger: fluid can collect and press on the heart (tamponade).
- **Myocarditis**: inflammation of the heart muscle → tiredness, breathlessness, chest pain, arrhythmias.
- **Endocarditis (infective)**: infection of the heart's inner lining and valves → fever, murmur, small emboli; needs long antibiotic treatment. People with valve disease take antibiotics before dental and surgical procedures to prevent it.
- **Cardiomyopathy**: disease of the heart muscle itself (dilated, hypertrophic or restrictive) → heart failure and arrhythmias.
- Nursing for all: rest, monitor vital signs and rhythm, give drugs on time, watch for failure and emboli, teach prevention.

## 5.8 Cardiac dysrhythmias and heart block

- **Dysrhythmia (arrhythmia)**: an abnormal heart rhythm — too fast, too slow or irregular.
- Examples: sinus tachycardia (fast), sinus bradycardia (slow), **atrial fibrillation** (fast irregular atria, risk of clots and stroke), ventricular tachycardia and **ventricular fibrillation** (life-threatening — the ventricles quiver and do not pump).
- **Heart block**: the signal from the atria to the ventricles is delayed or blocked; complete heart block gives a very slow pulse and fainting and may need a pacemaker.
- Nursing: continuous ECG monitoring, record the rhythm, note the pulse and blood pressure, keep emergency drugs and the defibrillator ready, care of a patient with a pacemaker (teach to avoid strong magnetic fields and to report dizziness or hiccups).

```text
Dangerous rhythms to recognise at once:
 Ventricular fibrillation → no effective pulse → start CPR, defibrillate
 Ventricular tachycardia without a pulse → treat like VF
 Asystole (flat line) → start CPR
```

## 5.9 Heart failure and related emergencies

### Congestive heart failure (CHF)

- The heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs, so blood backs up.
- **Left-sided failure**: blood backs up into the lungs → breathlessness, orthopnoea, night breathlessness, cough with frothy sputum, crackles.
- **Right-sided failure**: blood backs up into the body → swollen feet and sacrum, raised neck veins, enlarged tender liver, weight gain.
- Management: rest, oxygen, drugs as ordered (diuretics to remove fluid, drugs to strengthen or unload the heart), salt and fluid restriction.
- Nursing: sit the patient up (Fowler's position), oxygen, daily weight and strict intake–output, watch breathing and oxygen saturation, give drugs on time, low-salt diet, skin and pressure-area care, teach the patient to weigh daily and report weight gain and swelling.

### Cor pulmonale

- Right-sided heart failure caused by chronic lung disease (such as COPD). Care includes treating the lung disease, oxygen and the usual heart-failure care.

### Acute pulmonary oedema

- A sudden flooding of the lungs with fluid — an emergency. Severe breathlessness, pink frothy sputum, gasping, restlessness, fast pulse.
- Nursing: sit the patient upright with legs down, high-flow oxygen, call for help, give drugs as ordered, reassure, continuous monitoring.

### Cardiogenic shock

- Shock because the heart cannot pump (often after a large heart attack): low blood pressure, cold clammy skin, confusion, little urine. Needs intensive care, oxygen, drugs to support the heart and blood pressure, and continuous monitoring.

### Cardiac tamponade

- Fluid or blood collects in the pericardial sac and squeezes the heart so it cannot fill. Features (Beck's triad): low blood pressure, muffled heart sounds, raised neck veins. It is relieved by draining the fluid (pericardiocentesis). Nursing: recognise it, call for help, assist with drainage, monitor.

## 5.10 Cardiopulmonary arrest and BLS/BCLS

**Cardiopulmonary arrest** is the sudden stopping of effective breathing and heartbeat. Without blood flow the brain is damaged within minutes, so action must be immediate.

### Chain of survival

```text
Early recognition and call for help → Early CPR → Early defibrillation
   → Advanced care → Post-resuscitation care
```

### Basic Life Support (BLS) — the DRCAB/CAB approach

1. **Danger**: check the area is safe for you and the patient.
2. **Response**: tap and shout "Are you all right?"
3. **Call for help**: shout for help and the emergency team; send someone for the defibrillator (AED).
4. **Check breathing and pulse** (take no more than about 10 seconds). If not breathing normally and no pulse → start CPR.
5. **C — Compressions** (begin with these in an adult):
   - Place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone (centre of the chest), the other hand on top.
   - Push hard and fast: about 100–120 compressions a minute, depth about 5 cm, let the chest come fully back up each time.
   - Change the person giving compressions about every 2 minutes to avoid tiring.
6. **A — Airway**: open the airway by head tilt and chin lift (jaw thrust if neck injury is suspected).
7. **B — Breathing**: give rescue breaths with a bag-mask or mouth-to-mask; the chest should rise.
   - One rescuer, adult: 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
8. Continue CPR until the AED arrives, the patient recovers, or help takes over.

### Using an AED (automated external defibrillator)

- Switch it on and follow the spoken instructions; dry the chest, attach the pads as shown; stand clear while it analyses; if it advises a shock, make sure no one is touching the patient, then press shock; resume compressions at once.

### Basic Cardiac Life Support (BCLS) / advanced points

- Good-quality compressions with the fewest breaks are the most important factor in survival.
- A shockable rhythm (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) is treated with defibrillation; a non-shockable rhythm (asystole, pulseless electrical activity) is treated with continued CPR and emergency drugs by the team.
- Emergency drugs are given by the advanced team as per protocol (named by class only, not by dose here).
- After return of the heartbeat: keep the airway and oxygen, monitor, find and treat the cause, and transfer to intensive care.

**Nursing role in arrest**: recognise it early, call the code, start compressions without delay, bring the crash cart and defibrillator, assist the team, record times and actions, and support the family afterwards.

## Remember

- Blood flow: body → RA → RV → lungs → LA → LV → aorta → body. Pacemaker = SA node.
- After cardiac catheterisation: bed rest, pressure on the site, check distal pulse, colour and warmth; encourage fluids.
- Hypertension is the "silent killer"; take drugs for life even when feeling well; measure BP correctly.
- Angina pain is relieved by rest and nitroglycerine; heart attack pain is not.
- Heart attack first aid as ordered: MONA — Morphine, Oxygen, Nitroglycerine, Aspirin; continuous ECG, rest.
- Atrial fibrillation carries a risk of clots and stroke.
- Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless VT are shockable; asystole is not — but all need CPR.
- Left heart failure → lungs (breathlessness); right heart failure → body (oedema, raised neck veins). Daily weight is a key measure.
- Cardiac tamponade = Beck's triad: low BP, muffled heart sounds, raised neck veins.
- Adult CPR: push on the lower half of the sternum, 100–120/min, about 5 cm deep, 30 compressions to 2 breaths; change rescuers every 2 minutes; use the AED as soon as it arrives.
