# Unit 6: Nursing management of patients with disorders of blood and of the endocrine system

This notes file joins two short INC units: Unit VII (disorders of blood, 7 hours) and Unit VIII (disorders of the endocrine system, 8 hours). Both rely on blood tests, and diabetes mellitus (endocrine) is one of the most commonly asked topics in the whole course, so study the second half carefully.

---

## PART A — DISORDERS OF BLOOD

## 6.1 Review of anatomy and physiology of blood

- Blood is a connective tissue made of **plasma** (the fluid, about 55%) and **cells** (about 45%).
- Cells: **red blood cells (RBCs/erythrocytes)** carry oxygen using haemoglobin; **white blood cells (WBCs/leucocytes)** fight infection; **platelets (thrombocytes)** help clotting.
- Blood is made in the red bone marrow (haematopoiesis). RBCs live about 120 days and are broken down in the spleen and liver.
- Functions: transport (oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, wastes, hormones), defence (WBCs, antibodies), clotting, and keeping body temperature and pH steady.

| Normal value (adult, approximate) | Range |
| --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | Men about 13–17 g/dL; women about 12–15 g/dL |
| Total WBC count | 4,000–11,000 /µL |
| Platelet count | 1.5–4.0 lakh /µL (150,000–400,000) |

Use your own laboratory's reference range; values differ a little between labs.

## 6.2 Nursing assessment

**History**: tiredness, weakness, breathlessness, dizziness, bleeding or bruising easily, repeated infections, fever, bone pain, weight loss, diet (iron and vitamins), family history, blood loss (heavy periods, piles, ulcers).

**Physical assessment**: pallor (conjunctiva, nail beds, palms), jaundice, bruises (purpura, petechiae), bleeding gums, enlarged lymph nodes, enlarged spleen or liver, rapid pulse.

**Diagnostic tests**: complete blood count, peripheral blood smear, haemoglobin, reticulocyte count, bone marrow aspiration, clotting tests, blood grouping and cross-matching. Nurse's part: explain tests, label samples correctly, apply pressure after venepuncture, assist and care for the patient after bone marrow aspiration (pressure, watch for bleeding, rest).

## 6.3 Anaemia

**Anaemia** is a fall in haemoglobin (or RBCs) below normal, so less oxygen reaches the tissues. It is very common in India, especially in women.

| Type | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| Iron-deficiency | Blood loss, poor iron intake, pregnancy — the commonest |
| Megaloblastic | Lack of vitamin B12 or folic acid |
| Haemolytic | RBCs broken down too fast (e.g. thalassaemia, sickle cell) |
| Aplastic | Bone marrow fails to make cells |
| Anaemia of chronic disease | Long illness, kidney failure, cancer |

- Features: tiredness, weakness, breathlessness on effort, pallor, dizziness, fast pulse, poor concentration; a smooth sore tongue and spoon-shaped nails in iron deficiency.
- Management: find and treat the cause; iron or vitamin supplements, diet rich in iron (green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates, pulses, eggs, meat) and folate; blood transfusion if severe.
- Nursing: plan rest with activity, oxygen if very low, give iron with vitamin C for better absorption and warn that it darkens the stool, teach diet, treat the cause (deworming, treat ulcers, iron in pregnancy).

## 6.4 Polycythaemia

- Too many red cells make the blood thick, so it flows slowly and clots form.
- Features: red face, headache, dizziness, high blood pressure, risk of clots (stroke, DVT).
- Management: remove blood (venesection) as ordered, keep well hydrated, drugs as ordered.
- Nursing: encourage fluids, watch for signs of clotting, early movement.

## 6.5 Bleeding and clotting disorders

- **Clotting factor defects**: e.g. **haemophilia** (an inherited lack of a clotting factor) → bleeding into joints and muscles, prolonged bleeding after injury. Care: prevent injury, apply pressure and cold, give the missing factor as ordered, do not give intramuscular injections or aspirin, careful oral care.
- **Platelet defects** (**thrombocytopenia**): too few platelets → petechiae, bruises, bleeding gums, nose bleeds. Care: avoid injury and sharp objects, use a soft toothbrush, apply pressure after injections, watch for internal bleeding.
- **Thalassaemia**: an inherited disorder in which abnormal haemoglobin is made; children need repeated blood transfusions and iron is removed with chelating drugs. It is prevented by carrier testing and counselling before marriage/pregnancy.
- **Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)**: widespread clotting and then bleeding at the same time, seen in severe illness — an emergency managed in intensive care.

## 6.6 White cell disorders and cancers of the blood

- **Leukaemia**: cancer of white cells; the marrow is filled with abnormal cells, so normal cells fall → anaemia, repeated infection, easy bleeding, enlarged liver, spleen and lymph nodes, bone pain. Acute types are rapid; chronic types are slower. Treatment: chemotherapy, sometimes bone marrow transplant.
- **Leukopenia / agranulocytosis**: too few white cells → high risk of infection; the patient is kept in protective (reverse barrier) isolation.
- **Lymphoma**: cancer of the lymph nodes (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin) → painless swollen lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, weight loss; treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
- **Myeloma**: cancer of plasma cells in the marrow → bone pain, fractures, anaemia, kidney problems.

**Nursing care of the patient on chemotherapy or with low counts**: strict infection control and reverse barrier nursing, watch for fever and bleeding, mouth care, good nutrition, emotional support, safe handling of chemotherapy drugs and waste, manage nausea and hair loss with the patient's understanding.

**Health education on blood donation**: donors should be healthy adults within the accepted age and weight, with normal haemoglobin, no recent illness or risky exposure; donation is safe, the body replaces the blood, and one donation can help several patients. The nurse screens donors, cares for them during and after donation (rest, fluids, pressure on the site) and encourages voluntary donation.

---

## PART B — DISORDERS OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM

## 6.7 Review of anatomy and physiology of the endocrine system

- Endocrine glands pour **hormones** straight into the blood to control growth, metabolism, water and salt balance, the stress response and reproduction.

| Gland | Main hormones and action |
| --- | --- |
| Pituitary (in the brain) | The "master gland"; growth hormone, and hormones that control the thyroid, adrenals and sex glands; ADH (controls water) and oxytocin |
| Thyroid (neck) | Thyroxine (T4) and T3 — control the body's metabolic rate; calcitonin lowers calcium |
| Parathyroid (4 small glands behind the thyroid) | Parathormone — raises blood calcium |
| Adrenal (on the kidneys) | Cortex: cortisol (stress, sugar), aldosterone (salt and water), sex hormones; medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline |
| Pancreas (islets) | Insulin lowers blood sugar; glucagon raises it |

- Disorders are of two kinds: **too much** hormone (hyper-) or **too little** (hypo-), and sometimes **tumours** of the gland.

## 6.8 Nursing assessment

Ask about changes in weight, appetite, energy, mood, skin, hair, bowel habit, periods, tolerance of heat or cold, thirst and passing urine, and family history. On examination look at skin and hair, any neck swelling, weight, blood pressure, pulse and eyes. Tests include blood hormone levels, blood sugar, ultrasound and scans.

## 6.9 Disorders of the thyroid

### Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid; e.g. Graves' disease, goitre)

- Too much thyroid hormone speeds up the body.
- Features: weight loss with good appetite, fast pulse and palpitations, heat intolerance and sweating, nervousness and tremor, loose stools, bulging eyes (exophthalmos), a neck swelling (goitre).
- Management: anti-thyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or surgery (thyroidectomy).
- **Thyroid storm** is a dangerous, sudden worsening with very high fever, fast heart and confusion — an emergency.

### Hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid)

- Too little hormone slows the body.
- Features: weight gain, tiredness, cold intolerance, dry skin and hair, constipation, slow pulse, puffy face, slow thinking, heavy periods.
- Management: lifelong thyroid hormone replacement, taken daily; regular blood tests.

### Nursing care around thyroid surgery (thyroidectomy)

- **Before**: make the thyroid calm with drugs as ordered, teach the patient to support the neck when moving.
- **After**: semi-Fowler's position with the neck supported, watch for **bleeding** (check behind the neck and dressing), **breathing difficulty** (swelling pressing on the windpipe — keep a tracheostomy set ready), a **hoarse voice** (nerve injury), and **tetany** (tingling, spasm) from accidental removal of the parathyroids — keep calcium ready. Encourage gentle voice checks and later neck exercises.

## 6.10 Disorders of the parathyroid

- **Hyperparathyroidism**: too much parathormone → high blood calcium → weak bones, kidney stones, weakness, constipation, confusion.
- **Hypoparathyroidism**: too little → low calcium → tingling, muscle spasm (tetany), seizures; often after thyroid surgery. Managed with calcium and vitamin D.

## 6.11 Disorders of the adrenal and pituitary glands

- **Cushing's syndrome** (too much cortisol): round "moon" face, trunk obesity with thin limbs, purple stretch marks, high BP, high sugar, thin skin that bruises, weak bones, low mood.
- **Addison's disease** (too little adrenal hormone): weakness, weight loss, low BP, dark skin, salt craving; an **adrenal crisis** (sudden severe weakness, low BP, shock) is an emergency needing steroids and fluids.
- **Phaeochromocytoma** (adrenal medulla tumour): bursts of very high BP, headache, sweating, palpitations.
- **Pituitary disorders**: too much growth hormone causes gigantism (children) or acromegaly (adults, large hands, feet and jaw); too little ADH causes **diabetes insipidus** (passing large amounts of dilute urine and great thirst — different from diabetes mellitus).
- Nursing: monitor weight, BP, blood sugar and fluid balance; give hormone replacement exactly as ordered and teach that it must not be stopped suddenly; prepare for scans and surgery.

## 6.12 Diabetes mellitus (very important)

Diabetes mellitus is a long-term disorder in which blood sugar is high because the body makes too little insulin, or cannot use it well.

| Type | Features |
| --- | --- |
| **Type 1** | The pancreas makes little or no insulin; usually in young people; needs insulin for life |
| **Type 2** | The body resists insulin; usually in adults, linked to obesity and inactivity; managed with diet, exercise, tablets, and sometimes insulin — the common type in India |
| **Gestational** | First appears in pregnancy |

- **Classic features**: passing a lot of urine (polyuria), great thirst (polydipsia), increased hunger (polyphagia), weight loss, tiredness, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds and repeated infections.
- **Diagnosis**: raised fasting blood sugar, raised post-meal sugar, raised HbA1c (average sugar over about three months). Nurses monitor sugar with a glucometer (GRBS).

### Acute complications

- **Hypoglycaemia (low sugar)**: sudden sweating, shaking, hunger, fast pulse, confusion, then unconsciousness. It can follow too much insulin, a missed meal or extra exercise. **Treat at once**: if the patient can swallow, give sugar/glucose by mouth; if unconscious, nothing by mouth — give glucose by vein or glucagon as ordered and call for help. Remember the rule "when in doubt, give sugar," because low sugar harms the brain quickly.
- **Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA, mainly type 1)**: very high sugar with ketones → deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, dehydration, vomiting, drowsiness; an emergency treated with IV fluids, insulin and potassium as ordered.
- **Hyperosmolar state (mainly type 2)**: very high sugar with severe dehydration and confusion.

### Chronic complications

- Eyes (retinopathy, may cause blindness), kidneys (nephropathy), nerves (neuropathy — numb feet), heart and vessels (heart attack, stroke, poor leg circulation), and the diabetic foot (ulcers and gangrene from numbness and poor blood flow).

### Management and nursing care

- **Diet**: regular meals, complex carbohydrates and fibre, limit sugar and fried food, control weight — the nurse teaches a simple, affordable diabetic diet plan.
- **Exercise**: regular activity helps lower sugar; carry sugar in case it drops.
- **Drugs**: oral drugs for type 2; insulin for type 1 and when needed in type 2 (described, not dosed).
- **Insulin teaching (self-administration)**: store insulin properly (cool, not frozen), roll cloudy insulin gently (do not shake), use the correct syringe or pen, give under the skin (subcutaneous) in the abdomen, thigh or arm, **rotate the sites** to prevent lumps, keep to the timing with meals, and recognise and treat low sugar.
- **Monitoring**: teach home blood-sugar testing and record keeping.
- **Foot care**: wash and dry feet daily, check for cuts and blisters, wear well-fitting footwear, never walk barefoot, cut nails straight, treat any wound early.
- **Sick-day rules and follow-up**: do not stop insulin when ill, drink fluids, check sugar often, attend regular check-ups of eyes, kidneys and feet.

```text
Diabetes teaching — the key messages to a patient:
 Eat on time → Take medicine/insulin on time → Move daily
 → Test sugar → Care for feet → Know the signs of high and low sugar
```

## Remember

- Haemoglobin (adult): men ~13–17, women ~12–15 g/dL; platelets 1.5–4 lakh/µL.
- Iron-deficiency anaemia is the commonest; give iron with vitamin C; it darkens the stool.
- In thrombocytopenia and haemophilia: avoid injury and IM injections, use a soft toothbrush, apply pressure after venepuncture.
- Thalassaemia is prevented by carrier testing before marriage/pregnancy.
- Leukaemia and low white counts → reverse barrier (protective) nursing; watch for fever and bleeding.
- After thyroidectomy watch for: bleeding, breathing difficulty, hoarse voice and tetany; keep tracheostomy set and calcium ready.
- Hyperthyroidism speeds the body up (weight loss, fast pulse, heat intolerance); hypothyroidism slows it down.
- Diabetes classic signs: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss; HbA1c shows control over ~3 months.
- Hypoglycaemia is sudden and dangerous — when in doubt, give sugar; if unconscious, nothing by mouth.
- Insulin is given subcutaneously; rotate sites; store cool; roll cloudy insulin, do not shake.
- Diabetic foot care and daily foot checks prevent ulcers and amputation.

# Unit 7: Patients with disorders of the integumentary system

INC Unit VII covers skin anatomy and physiology, assessment, and nursing management of common skin conditions including eczema, psoriasis, urticaria, acne, infections, pressure ulcers and burns.

---

## 7.1 Anatomy and physiology of the skin

The skin (integument) is the largest organ of the body. It has three layers.

```text
SKIN LAYERS (cross-section)
─────────────────────────────────────────
Epidermis   │ outermost, avascular, 5 sub-layers
            │ Stratum corneum (dead keratinocytes)
            │ Stratum granulosum
            │ Stratum spinosum
            │ Stratum basale (mitosis, melanocytes)
─────────────────────────────────────────
Dermis      │ collagen + elastin fibres
            │ blood vessels, lymphatics
            │ hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous glands
            │ nerve endings (pain, touch, temperature)
─────────────────────────────────────────
Hypodermis  │ subcutaneous fat
(Subcutis)  │ insulation, shock absorption, energy store
─────────────────────────────────────────
```

**Functions of the skin**

| Function | How |
| --- | --- |
| Protection | Physical barrier against microorganisms, UV, chemicals |
| Thermoregulation | Sweating (cooling), vasoconstriction/dilation, fat insulation |
| Sensation | Receptors for pain, pressure, touch, temperature, vibration |
| Excretion | Salt and water via sweat |
| Vitamin D synthesis | UV converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 |
| Immunity | Langerhans cells present antigens |
| Fluid balance | Prevents water loss from internal tissues |

**Skin appendages**: hair follicles (cover and protection), sebaceous glands (secrete sebum, lubricate skin), sweat glands — eccrine (all over body, thermoregulation) and apocrine (axilla, groin, body odour after puberty), nails (protect tips of digits).

---

## 7.2 Nursing assessment of the skin

### History
Ask about: onset and duration of lesion, spread, itching or pain, previous skin disease, family history (psoriasis, eczema, atopy), allergies (food, drugs, latex, metals), occupation, cosmetics, home remedies, systemic diseases (diabetes, thyroid, autoimmune), medications, recent infections or travel.

### Physical assessment

Examine in good natural or bright light. Assess:
- **Colour**: normal, pallor (anaemia), cyanosis, jaundice (yellow), erythema (redness), pigmentation changes, vitiligo (depigmentation).
- **Temperature**: warm (infection, inflammation), cold (ischaemia).
- **Moisture**: dry, oily, sweaty.
- **Texture and turgor**: smooth vs rough; pinch the skin — slow return indicates dehydration.
- **Lesions**: describe using the correct terminology below.

**Primary lesions** (arise from normal skin):

| Lesion | Description | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Macule | Flat, colour change, <1 cm | Freckle, vitiligo |
| Patch | Flat, colour change, >1 cm | Port-wine stain |
| Papule | Raised, solid, <1 cm | Acne lesion, wart |
| Plaque | Raised, flat-topped, >1 cm | Psoriasis |
| Nodule | Raised, solid, >1 cm, deeper | Lipoma, rheumatoid nodule |
| Vesicle | Fluid-filled blister, <1 cm | Chickenpox, herpes |
| Bulla | Fluid-filled blister, >1 cm | Pemphigus, second-degree burn |
| Pustule | Pus-filled | Acne, folliculitis |
| Wheal (urtica) | Raised, transient, irregular edge | Urticaria |
| Cyst | Encapsulated, fluid/semisolid | Sebaceous cyst |

**Secondary lesions** (follow primary lesions or treatment): scales (psoriasis), crusts (impetigo), erosion, ulcer, fissure, scar, lichenification (thickened skin from chronic scratching).

### Diagnostic tests
Skin biopsy (histology), scraping for microscopy and culture (fungal/bacterial), patch test (contact allergy), Tzanck smear (viral), Wood's lamp (fluorescence in tinea/pityriasis), allergy scratch/prick test, CBC and immunology if systemic disease suspected.

---

## 7.3 Eczema (Dermatitis)

**Eczema** is a chronic, itching, inflammatory skin condition. It is not contagious.

**Types**

| Type | Trigger / feature | Key nursing point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Atopic eczema | Genetic; associated with asthma, hay fever; common in children | Avoid triggers, emollients, avoid scratching |
| Contact dermatitis (allergic) | Allergy to nickel, latex, cosmetics, plants | Identify and remove allergen; patch test |
| Contact dermatitis (irritant) | Soap, detergents, frequent hand-washing | Barrier cream, wear gloves |
| Seborrhoeic dermatitis | Yeast (Malassezia); affects scalp, face, chest | Antifungal shampoo, mild steroid cream |
| Nummular (discoid) eczema | Coin-shaped patches; dry skin, cold weather | Emollients, mild steroids |
| Stasis (varicose) eczema | Venous insufficiency; lower legs | Compression bandaging, treat venous disease |

**Features**: intense itching (pruritus), redness, vesicles (which weep and crust), lichenification from chronic scratching.

**Management**
- Identify and remove triggers.
- Emollients (moisturisers) — apply liberally and frequently; never use soap.
- Topical corticosteroids (mild for face/skin folds, moderate/strong for body) during flares; apply thinly.
- Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) for sensitive areas.
- Antihistamines for sleep disturbance.
- Systemic steroids or immunosuppressants (cyclosporin, methotrexate) for severe cases.
- Wet dressings to soothe acute weeping lesions.

**Nursing care**: keep nails short and clean, cool the environment, cotton clothing, avoid known triggers, teach proper application of emollients and steroids (finger-tip unit), avoid abrupt steroid withdrawal, monitor for secondary bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus, impetigo).

---

## 7.4 Psoriasis

**Psoriasis** is a chronic, immune-mediated disorder with accelerated keratinocyte turnover (normal 28 days → 3–4 days) causing thick silvery-white scales on erythematous plaques.

**Features**
- Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales; most common on elbows, knees, scalp and lower back.
- **Auspitz sign**: tiny bleeding points when scale is lifted.
- **Koebner phenomenon**: new plaques appear at sites of skin injury (scratch, tattoo, surgery).
- **Nail changes**: pitting, onycholysis (nail lifting), oil-drop sign.
- **Psoriatic arthritis** in 20–30%: affects joints, can cause deformity.

**Types**: plaque (most common), guttate (drop-like after Strep throat, common in children), inverse (skin folds), erythrodermic (whole body, emergency), pustular.

**Management**
- **Topical**: coal tar, dithranol, calcipotriol (vitamin D analogue), topical steroids, retinoids.
- **Phototherapy**: narrowband UVB (NB-UVB), PUVA (psoralen + UVA).
- **Systemic**: methotrexate, cyclosporin, acitretin (retinoid).
- **Biologics**: TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab), IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab) for severe disease.

**Nursing care**: apply thick emollients to soften scales before treatment, teach trigger avoidance (stress, infections, certain drugs — beta-blockers, lithium, NSAIDs, antimalarials), reassure that it is not contagious, support with psychosocial care (poor body image is common), monitor for side effects of methotrexate (liver, bone marrow — regular LFT and CBC).

---

## 7.5 Urticaria (Hives)

**Urticaria** is a superficial skin oedema from mast-cell histamine release, producing transient wheals (hives) and surrounding flare that disappear within 24 hours. **Angioedema** is deeper swelling of dermis/subcutis, commonly around eyes and lips; involvement of the larynx is life-threatening.

**Causes**: foods (nuts, shellfish, eggs, strawberries), drugs (penicillin, aspirin, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), latex, insect stings, infections, cold, pressure, exercise, idiopathic (most chronic urticaria).

**Management**
- Identify and avoid trigger.
- Non-sedating antihistamines (cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine) — first line, taken regularly not just when itchy.
- Sedating antihistamines (chlorpheniramine) for night-time relief.
- Short course of systemic corticosteroids for severe acute episodes.
- **Anaphylaxis / severe angioedema** (laryngeal oedema, bronchospasm, hypotension): adrenaline (epinephrine) 0.5 mg IM immediately (outer thigh), call emergency, oxygen, IV antihistamine, IV corticosteroid, monitor airway.

**Nursing**: teach patient to carry an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen) if at risk of anaphylaxis, wear a MedicAlert bracelet, recognise early warning signs.

---

## 7.6 Acne Vulgaris

**Acne** is a chronic disorder of the pilosebaceous unit (hair follicle + sebaceous gland), most common in adolescents.

**Pathogenesis**: androgen stimulation → increased sebum → Propionibacterium acnes (Cutibacterium acnes) colonises → inflammatory response → open comedones (blackheads, pore is open, sebum oxidises black), closed comedones (whiteheads), papules, pustules, nodules, cysts → scarring.

**Management** (stepwise by severity)

| Severity | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Mild (comedones, few papules) | Topical benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids (adapalene), topical clindamycin |
| Moderate (papules, pustules) | As above + oral antibiotics (doxycycline, erythromycin 6–8 weeks) |
| Severe/nodular/cystic | Oral isotretinoin (retinoid — very effective, teratogenic: mandatory contraception in females, monthly LFT and lipids) |
| In females with hormonal acne | Combined oral contraceptive pill, anti-androgens (spironolactone) |

**Nursing care**: wash face gently twice daily with a mild soap-free cleanser, do not squeeze lesions (drives infection deeper, causes scars), apply topical treatment as a thin layer over the whole area not just on spots, sun protection with isotretinoin and topical retinoids, support self-image in adolescents.

---

## 7.7 Skin infections

**Bacterial**
- **Impetigo**: very contagious superficial infection (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus); honey-coloured crusts around mouth in children; topical mupirocin or oral antibiotics (flucloxacillin); separate towels and clothing.
- **Cellulitis**: spreading infection of dermis and subcutaneous tissue (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus); red, warm, swollen, tender skin, often on a leg; fever, lymphangitis; IV penicillin or cephalosporin; mark the edge to monitor spread; elevate the limb.
- **Erysipelas**: superficial cellulitis with well-defined raised edge; treated the same way.
- **Folliculitis**: infection of hair follicles; furuncle (boil) is a deep infection; carbuncle is confluent boils; topical antiseptic or antibiotics; warm compresses; incision and drainage for fluctuant boils; avoid shaving over affected area.

**Fungal (Tinea / Dermatophytosis)**
- Tinea pedis (athlete's foot), tinea corporis (ringworm), tinea capitis (scalp), tinea unguium (onychomycosis).
- Diagnosis: Wood's lamp (some species fluoresce), KOH scraping (fungal hyphae).
- Treatment: topical antifungals (clotrimazole, miconazole) for body/foot; oral antifungals (terbinafine, fluconazole) for scalp or nails; keep skin dry, cotton socks, shared footwear avoided.

**Viral**
- **Herpes zoster (shingles)**: reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in a dermatomal strip (unilateral); burning pain, then vesicular rash; oral aciclovir within 72 h reduces severity; analgesics; post-herpetic neuralgia; contact precautions.
- **Warts (verrucae)**: HPV; treated with salicylic acid, cryotherapy, electrocautery; will often clear spontaneously.
- **Molluscum contagiosum**: poxvirus; pearly, umbilicated papules; resolves without treatment.

**Infestations**
- **Scabies**: Sarcoptes scabiei mite burrowing into skin; intense itching worse at night; linear burrows between fingers, wrists, genitalia; treat the whole family simultaneously with permethrin 5% cream head to toe for 8–12 hours; wash all clothes and bedding at 60 °C; treat close contacts.
- **Pediculosis (lice)**: head, body, pubic; malathion or permethrin shampoo; fine comb; treat household contacts.

---

## 7.8 Pressure ulcers (Pressure injuries)

A **pressure ulcer** (decubitus ulcer, bed sore) is localised injury to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, from sustained pressure or pressure combined with shear/friction.

**Risk factors**: immobility, poor nutrition (low protein), incontinence (moisture), altered sensation (spinal injury, neuropathy), low blood pressure, old age, oedema.

**Assessment tool — Braden Scale** (6 categories each scored 1–4; lowest score = highest risk):
Sensory perception, Moisture, Activity, Mobility, Nutrition, Friction and shear. Score ≤18 = at risk; ≤12 = very high risk.

**Common sites**: sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, trochanters, occiput, medial malleoli, elbows.

**Staging (NPUAP/EPUAP)**

| Stage | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Stage 1 | Non-blanchable erythema; skin intact; may be warmer/firmer |
| Stage 2 | Partial-thickness loss of dermis; shallow open ulcer; pink wound bed, blister or serosanguineous wound |
| Stage 3 | Full-thickness skin loss into subcutaneous tissue; fat may be visible; no bone, tendon or muscle exposed |
| Stage 4 | Full-thickness loss with exposed bone, tendon or muscle; slough or eschar may be present |
| Unstageable | Full-thickness loss; slough or eschar obscures depth |
| Deep tissue injury | Purple/maroon localised area; intact or open blister; damaged by intense pressure/shear |

**Prevention** — the 5 Ps:
1. **Position change** every 2 hours; use a turning schedule; head of bed <30° unless contraindicated.
2. **Pressure-relieving surfaces**: special foam mattress, alternating-pressure mattress, heel offloading.
3. **Proper skin care**: keep skin dry but not dry enough to crack; barrier cream; moisture-wicking pads for incontinence.
4. **Protein and nutrition**: adequate protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day), vitamin C and zinc for healing; dietitian referral.
5. **Patient and family education**: the causes, signs and reporting.

**Treatment**
- Remove pressure completely.
- Wound assessment: dimensions, bed colour (red = healthy granulation; yellow = slough; black = eschar), odour, exudate, undermining.
- Wound cleaning: normal saline or clean running water; avoid antiseptics (cytotoxic to healing tissue).
- Dressings: hydrocolloid (moist healing, Stage 2), foam (exudate absorption), alginate (heavy exudate), silver dressings (infection), vacuum-assisted closure (Stage 3–4).
- Debridement of slough/eschar: sharp, enzymatic or autolytic.
- Treat infection: systemic antibiotics if signs of cellulitis/osteomyelitis.
- Nutritional support.
- Surgical closure (flap) for large deep ulcers.

---

## 7.9 Burns

### Classification of burns

**By depth**

| Depth | Old name | Features | Healing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Superficial (epidermal) | First degree | Red, dry, painful; epidermis only | 3–5 days; no scar |
| Superficial partial-thickness | Second degree (superficial) | Red/pink, moist, blistered, very painful | 10–14 days; minimal scar |
| Deep partial-thickness | Second degree (deep) | Pale/white/mottled, less painful (nerve damage), dry/wet | 3–8 weeks; scarring |
| Full-thickness | Third degree | White/grey/leathery/charred; painless (nerves destroyed) | Needs grafting; scar |
| Full-thickness + underlying tissues | Fourth degree | Bone, tendon, muscle involved | Needs reconstruction |

**By extent — Rule of Nines (adults)**

```text
              HEAD & NECK = 9%
           ┌──────────────────┐
           │      9%          │
      ─────┤                  ├─────
ARM 9% │  │   TRUNK          │  │ ARM 9%
       │  │  Front 18%       │  │
       │  │  Back  18%       │  │
      ─────┤                  ├─────
           │                  │
           │  PERINEUM = 1%   │
      ─────┴──────────────────┴─────
   LEG 18%                    LEG 18%
  (front 9%                 (front 9%
   back 9%)                  back 9%)
─────────────────────────────────────
Total body surface area (TBSA) = 100%
```

Children use the **Lund–Browder chart** (more accurate because head is proportionally larger in children).

**Palm method**: patient's palm (fingers together) = approximately 1% TBSA; useful for scattered burns.

### Burn first aid
1. Remove from source; stop, drop and roll for flames.
2. Cool the burn: running cool (not cold/iced) water for 20 minutes; do not apply butter, toothpaste or ice.
3. Remove jewellery and loose clothing near the burn (not stuck clothing).
4. Cover with clean cling film or a non-fluffy dressing.
5. Keep the patient warm (hypothermia risk).
6. Refer to burns unit if: >10% TBSA (adults), >5% TBSA (children/elderly), full-thickness, face/hands/feet/genitalia/major joints, electrical/chemical/inhalation burns.

### Acute burn management (the 4 Rs)

**1. Resuscitation**
- **Parkland formula**: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA burned of Hartmann's (Ringer's lactate) in the first 24 hours; give half in the first 8 hours (counted from time of burn), the rest over the next 16 hours.
- Monitor urine output (target 0.5–1 mL/kg/h via catheter); adjust fluids accordingly.
- Nil by mouth initially (ileus), then nasogastric tube feeding.

**2. Resuscitation of the airway**
- Suspect inhalation injury: singed nasal hairs, hoarse voice, stridor, carbonaceous sputum, burns inside mouth.
- Airway must be secured early — oedema worsens in first 6–8 hours; intubation before the airway closes.
- 100% oxygen for suspected carbon monoxide poisoning; Carboxyhaemoglobin test.

**3. Wound care**
- Clean gently with chlorhexidine or mild soap and water; remove blisters (deep ones only).
- Topical antimicrobials: silver sulfadiazine 1% cream, silver-containing dressings (moist wound healing, reduce infection).
- **Escharotomy**: incision through eschar of circumferential full-thickness burns of limbs or chest to relieve compartment syndrome and allow chest movement.
- **Skin grafting**: split-thickness skin graft (STSG) — donor site taken with a dermatome; graft fixed on debrided wound; cultured skin or artificial dermis (Integra) for large burns.

**4. Rehabilitation**
- Early splinting and positioning to prevent contractures.
- Physiotherapy and occupational therapy.
- Pressure garments (worn 23 h/day for 1–2 years) to minimise hypertrophic scarring.
- Psychological support — burns cause major body image change, PTSD, depression.
- Nutritional support: high protein, high calorie (burns are hypermetabolic).

### Nursing care plan for a burn patient

| Problem | Nursing goal | Interventions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Impaired skin integrity | Wound healing; prevent infection | Aseptic wound care, topical antimicrobials, secure dressings, monitor for wound infection (fever, purulent discharge, cellulitis) |
| Risk for fluid volume deficit | Adequate hydration | Maintain Parkland resuscitation, accurate intake-output, hourly urine output, daily weight, IV access (large-bore) |
| Risk for infection | Prevent sepsis | Strict asepsis, barrier nursing, barrier cream, monitor wound and blood cultures, antibiotics as ordered |
| Acute pain | Pain control | Analgesia (opioids IV for major burns), pre-medicate before dressing changes, position of comfort, diversion |
| Impaired nutrition | Adequate calories and protein | NG tube feeding, dietitian input, high-protein high-calorie diet, vitamin C and zinc supplementation |
| Risk for contracture | Maintain range of movement | Splinting and positioning (see physiotherapy), early ROM exercises, pressure garments |
| Body image disturbance | Positive self-concept | Acknowledge feelings, involve in care, refer to support group and counsellor, gradual mirror exposure |

---

## 7.10 Skin cancers

| Type | Key features | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) | Commonest; pearly nodule with rolled edges, telangiectasia; sun-exposed areas; local invasion only, rarely metastasises | Surgery, radiotherapy, topical imiquimod or 5-FU for superficial type |
| Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) | Second commonest; arises in sun-damaged/scarred skin or actinic keratosis; can metastasise | Surgery, radiotherapy, Mohs for facial lesions |
| Malignant melanoma | Most dangerous; arises from melanocytes; ABCDEs: Asymmetry, irregular Border, Colour variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution; spreads early via lymph and blood | Wide local excision + sentinel lymph node biopsy, immunotherapy (nivolumab), targeted therapy (BRAF inhibitors) |

**Sun protection teaching**: SPF 30+, broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, avoid midday sun, examine skin monthly (ABCDE), report changes to a doctor.

---

## 7.11 Remember

- Skin layers: epidermis (avascular) → dermis (vascular, nerves, glands) → hypodermis (fat).
- Pressure ulcer prevention: 2-hourly turns, pressure-relieving mattress, adequate protein.
- Burns rule of nines: head 9%, each arm 9%, trunk front 18%, trunk back 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1%.
- Parkland formula: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA burned of Hartmann's in 24 hours; half in first 8 hours.
- Full-thickness burn: painless (nerve ends destroyed), waxy/leathery/charred; needs grafting.
- Anaphylaxis: adrenaline 0.5 mg IM first, then antihistamine + steroid.
- Psoriasis: Koebner phenomenon, Auspitz sign, silvery plaque; not infectious.
- Atopic eczema: itchy rash in flexures; associated with asthma and hay fever.
- Scabies: itching worst at night; treat whole family and wash all bedding.

# Unit 8: Patients with musculoskeletal problems

INC Unit VIII covers anatomy and physiology of the musculoskeletal system, nursing assessment, and care of patients with fractures, dislocations, infections of bone, metabolic bone disease, and joint disorders.

---

## 8.1 Anatomy and physiology

### Bone
- Functions: support, protection, movement (with muscles), calcium/phosphate storage, haematopoiesis (red marrow).
- Types: long (femur, humerus), short (carpals, tarsals), flat (skull, scapula, ribs), irregular (vertebrae, pelvis), sesamoid (patella).
- Structure: outer **periosteum** (vascular, pain-sensitive, contains osteoblasts for healing) → compact cortical bone → cancellous (spongy/trabecular) bone → bone marrow cavity.
- Cells: **osteoblasts** (form bone), **osteocytes** (maintain matrix), **osteoclasts** (resorb bone).
- Blood supply: nutrient artery enters via nutrient foramen; periosteal vessels supply the outer layers — both are needed for healing.

### Joints
- **Fibrous** (sutures of skull — no movement), **cartilaginous** (symphysis pubis, intervertebral discs — slight movement), **synovial** (most limb joints — freely movable).
- Synovial joint: articular cartilage (smooth, avascular) + joint capsule + synovial membrane (makes synovial fluid — lubricates and nourishes cartilage) + ligaments.

### Muscles
- Skeletal (voluntary) muscle — movement; attached to bone via tendons.
- Cardiac (involuntary).
- Smooth (involuntary) — hollow organs.
- **Origin** (fixed end, less movement) and **insertion** (moving end).

### Normal musculoskeletal values
- Adult bone density: T-score >−1 (normal by DEXA); −1 to −2.5 = osteopenia; <−2.5 = osteoporosis.
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): elevated in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), osteomyelitis, bone tumours.

---

## 8.2 Nursing assessment

**History**: onset (sudden = trauma/fracture vs gradual = arthritis), pain character (site, severity, radiation, what worsens/relieves), swelling, deformity, reduced range of motion, weakness, stiffness (morning stiffness of RA), previous fractures, occupational or sporting injury, osteoporosis risk (menopause, steroids, smoking, alcohol, low BMI, family history).

**Physical assessment**:
- Look: deformity, swelling, bruising, skin colour/integrity, posture, gait.
- Feel: warmth, tenderness (localised = fracture site), muscle spasm.
- Move: active then passive range of movement, crepitus (grating = bone ends), joint laxity.
- Special tests (by physiotherapist/doctor): valgus/varus stress, McMurray (knee meniscus), Lachman (ACL).
- Neurovascular status of limb distal to injury: **5 Ps** — Pain, Pulse, Pallor, Paraesthesia, Paralysis.

**Investigations**: X-ray (most fractures), CT (complex fractures, spine), MRI (soft tissue, ligament, meniscus, infection), bone scan, DEXA (bone density), ESR, CRP, RF (rheumatoid arthritis), uric acid (gout), blood culture (osteomyelitis).

---

## 8.3 Fractures

A **fracture** is a break in the continuity of bone. It is caused by trauma, repeated stress (stress fracture) or disease weakening the bone (pathological fracture).

### Types of fractures

| Type | Description | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Closed (simple) | Skin intact over fracture site | Most common; safer |
| Open (compound) | Bone penetrates or is near a skin wound; infection risk | High-velocity injuries |
| Greenstick | Incomplete fracture; one cortex intact; like bending a green twig | Children |
| Comminuted | Bone shattered into multiple fragments | High-energy trauma |
| Transverse | Fracture line perpendicular to long axis | Direct blow |
| Oblique | Fracture at an angle | Rotational force |
| Spiral | Fracture winds around the bone | Twisting injury (classic in child abuse) |
| Compression | Vertebral body crushed | Osteoporosis, fall from height |
| Avulsion | Bone fragment pulled off by tendon/ligament | Ankle, pelvis |
| Stress (fatigue) | Repeated microtrauma — no single event | March fracture (metatarsal in soldiers/runners) |
| Pathological | Bone already weakened (osteoporosis, tumour, Paget's) | Minimal or no trauma |

### Fracture healing stages

```text
1. HAEMATOMA (hours–days)
   Blood fills the fracture gap → clots → inflammatory reaction

2. SOFT CALLUS (1–2 weeks)
   Fibroblasts and osteoblasts invade → fibrocartilage bridge forms
   The fracture is still mobile but no longer freely moving

3. HARD CALLUS (3–6 weeks)
   Fibrocartilage replaced by woven bone (primary callus)
   Visible on X-ray

4. BONE REMODELLING (months–years)
   Woven bone → mature lamellar bone; medullary canal reopens
   Shape returns to near-normal (Wolff's law — bone remodels along stress lines)
```

Healing is affected by: age (faster in children), blood supply, bone type (cancellous heals faster than cortical), infection, immobilisation (inadequate = non-union), nutrition (calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, protein), systemic diseases (diabetes, steroids).

### Fracture management

**Principles**: Recognition → Resuscitation → Reduction → Immobilisation → Rehabilitation.

**1. First aid**
- Do not move the patient until the fracture is splinted.
- Splint in the position found; use a padded board, SAM splint or improvised splint.
- Control bleeding with pressure.
- Cover open fractures with a clean damp dressing (do not push bone back).
- Monitor neurovascular status (5 Ps) before and after splinting.

**2. Reduction**: realigning bone ends.
- **Closed reduction**: manipulation under anaesthesia (MUA).
- **Open reduction** (ORIF — open reduction and internal fixation): surgical; screws, plates, intramedullary nail, wires.

**3. Immobilisation methods**

| Method | Use | Nursing points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plaster of Paris (POP) cast | Simple fractures | Check circulation distal to cast; keep cast dry; do not put objects inside to scratch |
| Synthetic (fibreglass) cast | Simple fractures | Lighter, waterproof, sets faster |
| Traction | Femoral shaft, cervical spine, to reduce muscle spasm | Maintain correct weight and alignment; care for traction pin sites; prevent foot drop |
| External fixator | Open fractures, infected fractures, complex fractures | Pin site care (clean daily with saline/antiseptic, monitor for infection), keep fixator clean |
| Internal fixation (ORIF) | Displaced fractures, joint fractures | Post-operative nursing — wound, DVT prevention, early mobilisation |

**Cast nursing care**
- Elevate the limb above the heart for the first 24–48 hours to reduce swelling.
- **5 Ps** check every 1–2 hours initially; report pain unrelieved by analgesia (compartment syndrome).
- Keep cast dry (cover with plastic bag for showering).
- Do not use objects to scratch inside the cast.
- Report: increased pain, numbness, pallor, cold fingers/toes, cast cracking or smelling (possible wound infection or pressure sore under cast).
- Teach cast care: signs to report, activity restrictions, follow-up X-ray dates.

### Complications of fractures

| Complication | Signs | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compartment syndrome | Severe pain unrelieved by analgesia, pain on passive stretch of muscles, tight tense limb, paraesthesia, pallor | Emergency: notify surgeon immediately; remove all encircling bandages/cast; fasciotomy if pressure >30 mmHg |
| Fat embolism syndrome | 24–72 hours post-long-bone fracture or manipulation; petechial rash, confusion, hypoxia, tachycardia; fat globules in urine | Oxygen, supportive care, corticosteroids, early mobilisation or fixation |
| Avascular necrosis | Loss of blood supply to bone fragment (femoral head after hip fracture, scaphoid) | Surgical |
| Non-union / delayed union | Fracture not healed at expected time | Bone grafting, electrical stimulation |
| Malunion | Fracture heals in wrong position | Osteotomy |
| Infection (osteomyelitis) | In open fractures | Antibiotics, debridement |
| DVT / pulmonary embolism | Lower limb fractures, immobility | Anticoagulation, compression stockings, early mobilisation |

---

## 8.4 Dislocations

A **dislocation** is complete loss of contact between joint surfaces; a **subluxation** is partial loss.

Common sites: shoulder (commonest dislocation), elbow, hip (congenital hip dysplasia in infants), patella, ankle.

**Features**: deformity, pain, inability to move, swelling; loss of normal joint contour.

**Management**: X-ray first (rule out fracture), then reduction under analgesia/sedation; immobilise; physiotherapy to regain strength.

---

## 8.5 Osteomyelitis

**Osteomyelitis** is infection of bone. The commonest organism is **Staphylococcus aureus**.

**Routes**: haematogenous (blood-borne spread from skin boil, UTI, dental abscess — common in children, affects metaphysis of long bones), direct (open fracture, surgery, joint replacement), contiguous (from adjacent soft tissue infection).

**Types**

| Type | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Acute | Sudden onset; fever, local pain, warmth, swelling, reduced movement; child refuses to weight-bear |
| Chronic | Following incompletely treated acute; dead bone (sequestrum), shell of new bone (involucrum), sinus tract discharging pus |

**Investigations**: raised WBC, CRP, ESR; blood culture (take before antibiotics); X-ray (changes appear after 10–14 days — periosteal elevation), MRI (early detection), bone scan.

**Management**
- Prolonged IV antibiotics (4–6 weeks minimum; flucloxacillin for Staphylococcus); then oral.
- Rest and splinting of the affected limb.
- Surgical debridement (removal of dead bone/pus) for chronic osteomyelitis or if no response.
- Wound irrigation and dressings for open wounds.

**Nursing care**: immobilise and elevate the limb, strict asepsis during dressing changes, wound irrigation as ordered, monitor vital signs and inflammatory markers, ensure complete antibiotic course (never stop early), nutritional support, psychological support in long illness, teach signs of relapse.

---

## 8.6 Bone tumours

| Type | Features | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Osteosarcoma | Most common primary malignant bone tumour; adolescents; distal femur/proximal tibia; Codman's triangle on X-ray; "sunray" spicules | Limb-sparing surgery + chemotherapy |
| Ewing's sarcoma | Children; diaphysis of long bones; "onion skin" periosteal reaction on X-ray | Chemotherapy + surgery or radiotherapy |
| Osteochondroma | Commonest benign tumour; bony outgrowth with cartilage cap; near growth plates; most left alone unless symptomatic | Excision if symptomatic |
| Multiple myeloma | Malignant plasma cells in bone marrow; "punched-out" lesions on X-ray; in older adults; bone pain, anaemia, renal failure, hypercalcaemia | Chemotherapy, biphosphonates |

**Nursing**: pain management (opioids for malignant bone pain), handle bones carefully (pathological fracture risk), calcium monitoring, teach side effects of chemotherapy, psychological support.

---

## 8.7 Osteoporosis

**Osteoporosis** is reduced bone mass and strength leading to fragile bones and fracture risk.

**Risk factors**: female sex, post-menopause (oestrogen loss accelerates bone resorption), age >65, family history, low BMI, smoking, excess alcohol, low calcium/vitamin D intake, long-term corticosteroids, thyroid excess, sedentary lifestyle.

**Features**: often silent until a fracture occurs; typical fractures: wrist (Colles'), vertebral (wedge, can cause kyphosis and loss of height), hip (neck of femur — most dangerous; high mortality).

**Diagnosis**: DEXA scan — T-score ≤−2.5.

**Management**
- **Non-pharmacological**: weight-bearing exercise (walking, dancing — builds bone), fall prevention (home assessment, grab rails, good footwear, eye care), calcium (1000–1200 mg/day) and vitamin D (800–1000 IU/day).
- **Pharmacological**: bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate — take with full glass of water, sit upright for 30 min; osteonecrosis of jaw is a rare serious side effect), denosumab (RANK-L inhibitor, injection every 6 months), teriparatide (PTH analogue, stimulates new bone formation), HRT (post-menopausal women, short-term).

**Nursing**: teach fracture risk and prevention, medication compliance (bisphosphonate instructions are critical), calcium and vitamin D supplementation, home safety assessment, exercise programme, screen for depression (chronic pain, loss of independence).

---

## 8.8 Rheumatoid arthritis versus osteoarthritis

**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)** is a systemic autoimmune disease causing symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis with joint destruction.

**Osteoarthritis (OA)** is a degenerative joint disease from cartilage breakdown, most common in weight-bearing joints.

| Feature | Rheumatoid Arthritis | Osteoarthritis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Autoimmune — synovitis; pannus erodes cartilage | Wear and tear; cartilage loss, subchondral sclerosis |
| Age | Any age; peak 30–50; more females | >50; both sexes equally (older age) |
| Joints | Symmetrical; small joints first (MCP, PIP, wrists) | Asymmetrical; weight-bearing (knees, hips), DIPs of hands, spine |
| Morning stiffness | >1 hour; relieved by activity | <30 minutes; "gelling" after rest |
| Swelling | Soft (synovitis, effusion) | Hard (osteophytes), Heberden's nodes (DIP), Bouchard's (PIP) |
| Systemic features | Fatigue, fever, anaemia, rheumatoid nodules, vasculitis, lung disease | None — purely articular |
| X-ray | Periarticular osteoporosis, joint space narrowing, erosions | Osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, joint space narrowing, subchondral cysts |
| Serology | RF positive (70%), anti-CCP (more specific) | Negative |
| Treatment | DMARDs (methotrexate first line), biologic agents (TNF inhibitors), NSAIDs, steroids | Simple analgesics (paracetamol), NSAIDs, physiotherapy, weight loss, joint replacement |

**Nursing care for RA**
- Rest affected joints during flares; splinting of wrists overnight.
- Gentle range-of-motion (ROM) exercises during remission; physiotherapy.
- Teach joint protection: use larger joints, avoid sustained grip, use aids (jar openers, raised toilet seat).
- Monitor for methotrexate toxicity: regular LFT and CBC; ensure folic acid supplementation; advise against alcohol.
- Support body image and functional independence; occupational therapy referral.

---

## 8.9 Low back pain and intervertebral disc herniation

**Low back pain** (LBP) is very common. Most (>90%) is mechanical (muscle strain, poor posture, disc degeneration); a few cases are due to serious causes (fracture, infection, malignancy) — red flags: age >50, history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, fever, night sweats, neurological deficit, bladder/bowel involvement (cauda equina emergency).

**Intervertebral disc herniation** ("slipped disc"): nucleus pulposus protrudes through the annulus fibrosus and presses on a nerve root → sciatica (pain radiating down the leg, usually below the knee in L4–L5/L5–S1 disc).

**Management of LBP**
- Short-term rest (not prolonged bed rest — worsens outcome); gentle early activity.
- Paracetamol, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants.
- Physiotherapy: core strengthening, posture correction, manual therapy.
- Epidural steroid injection for radicular pain.
- Surgery (discectomy, laminectomy) for persistent neurological deficit or cauda equina syndrome.

**Nursing**: encourage activity within pain limits, correct body mechanics (bend knees not waist, hold load close to body), mattress advice (medium-firm), pain management, encourage weight loss, occupational advice.

---

## 8.10 Rehabilitation principles

Rehabilitation begins the day after surgery or stabilisation of the fracture — not after full healing.

Goals: prevent complications of immobility (DVT, pressure ulcers, pneumonia, muscle wasting), restore range of motion, strength and function, enable return to independent living.

**Nurse's role**
- Passive and active ROM exercises.
- Positioning (foot drop prevention: foot board, calf rests).
- DVT prophylaxis: low-molecular-weight heparin, anti-embolism stockings, ankle pump exercises.
- Pressure ulcer prevention: turning, padding.
- Nutritional support.
- Encourage and supervise physiotherapy programme.
- Assistive devices: crutches, walking frame, wheelchair; teach safe use.
- Psychosocial support; referral to social work for home adaptations.

---

## 8.11 Remember

- **5 Ps** for neurovascular check: Pain, Pulse, Pallor, Paraesthesia, Paralysis.
- Fracture healing: haematoma → soft callus → hard callus → remodelling.
- Compartment syndrome = emergency: cut/bivalve cast, call surgeon for fasciotomy.
- Fat embolism: 24–72 h post-long-bone fracture; petechiae, confusion, hypoxia.
- Open fracture: cover with clean damp dressing; IV antibiotics; risk of osteomyelitis.
- Osteoporosis: DEXA T-score ≤−2.5; bisphosphonate — take with full glass of water and stay upright.
- RA vs OA: RA = autoimmune, symmetric, small joints, RF+, morning stiffness >1 h; OA = wear and tear, weight-bearing joints, Heberden's nodes.
- Osteomyelitis: Staphylococcus aureus; IV antibiotics 4–6 weeks; never stop early.

# Unit 9: Patients with communicable diseases

INC Unit IX covers infection control principles and the nursing management of common communicable diseases seen in India and globally, including HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, malaria, typhoid and dengue.

---

## 9.1 Principles of infection control

**Chain of infection**: Infectious agent → Reservoir → Portal of exit → Mode of transmission → Portal of entry → Susceptible host.

**Breaking the chain** at any link prevents infection.

### Standard precautions (apply to ALL patients, regardless of diagnosis)
- **Hand hygiene**: 5 moments (before patient contact, before aseptic task, after body fluid exposure, after patient contact, after contact with patient surroundings). WHO 6-step technique with soap and water (20 seconds) or alcohol hand rub (minimum 20 seconds).
- **PPE**: gloves (whenever touching blood/body fluids/mucous membranes/non-intact skin), mask and eye protection/face shield (risk of splash), gown (if clothing likely to be soiled).
- **Safe sharps handling**: never recap needles; use a sharps container; needle-stick protocol if injury occurs.
- **Safe handling of linen and waste**: red bags for infectious waste; yellow bags/sharps containers for sharps.
- **Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette**: mask patients with respiratory symptoms; cover cough.
- **Safe patient care equipment**: single-use items; decontaminate reusable equipment.

### Transmission-based precautions

| Category | Transmission route | Diseases | Precautions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Contact | Direct or indirect contact | MRSA, C. difficile, scabies, wound infections | Gloves + gown for all contact; dedicated equipment; private room or cohort |
| Droplet | Large droplets, <1 m | Influenza, meningococcal meningitis, mumps, rubella, pertussis | Surgical mask within 1 m; private room or curtain |
| Airborne | Small droplet nuclei, travel >1 m | Pulmonary TB, measles, chickenpox | N95/FFP2 respirator; negative-pressure room if available; private room |

---

## 9.2 HIV/AIDS

**HIV** (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) infects and destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes (helper T cells), progressively weakening immunity until opportunistic infections and AIDS develop.

### Transmission
- Sexual intercourse (unprotected; highest risk anal sex).
- Blood and blood products: shared needles (intravenous drug use), blood transfusion (now screened), needle-stick injury (risk ~0.3%).
- Mother to child (MTCT): during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding.
- **HIV is NOT transmitted** by: casual contact, coughing, sneezing, sharing food/utensils, mosquito bites, toilet seats.

### Stages (WHO/CDC)

| Stage | CD4 count | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary infection (acute HIV) | Variable (may fall initially) | Flu-like illness 2–4 weeks after infection; seroconversion illness |
| Asymptomatic (clinical latency) | 500–350 cells/µL (falling slowly) | No symptoms; virus replicates; lasts years without treatment |
| Symptomatic HIV | 350–200 cells/µL | Minor opportunistic infections; weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, oral candidiasis, shingles |
| AIDS | <200 cells/µL | Major opportunistic infections (see below); AIDS-defining cancers |

### Opportunistic infections

| Organ | Infection | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lungs | Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) | Dry cough, progressive breathlessness; treated with co-trimoxazole |
| Brain | Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal meningitis | Headache, altered consciousness; Cryptococcus: headache, stiff neck, positive India ink stain of CSF |
| Mouth/oesophagus | Candidiasis | White plaques; dysphagia; treated with fluconazole |
| Intestine | Cryptosporidiosis | Profuse watery diarrhoea |
| Skin | Kaposi's sarcoma | Painless purple/red skin lesions; AIDS-defining |
| Eyes | CMV retinitis | Blurred vision; can cause blindness |
| Systemic | Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) | Fever, weight loss, diarrhoea; in very low CD4 counts |

### Diagnosis
- **ELISA** (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay): screening test; detects antibodies; false negative in window period (3–6 weeks after infection before antibodies form).
- **Western blot**: confirmatory test.
- **Rapid HIV tests**: point-of-care; result in 20 minutes; needs confirmation.
- **Viral load** (HIV RNA PCR): measures amount of virus; used to monitor treatment.
- **CD4 count**: monitors immune status; guides when to start treatment.

The **window period** (infection to detectable antibodies): 3–6 weeks with 4th generation tests; during this time the person can still transmit HIV.

### Antiretroviral therapy (ART)

**Principle**: ART does not cure HIV but suppresses viral load to undetectable, allows CD4 recovery, prevents progression and transmission. **Treatment as prevention**: undetectable = untransmittable (U=U).

**Drug classes**

| Class | Examples | Site of action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) | Tenofovir (TDF), lamivudine (3TC), zidovudine (AZT) | Block reverse transcriptase (DNA synthesis from viral RNA) |
| Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) | Efavirenz, nevirapine | Directly inhibit reverse transcriptase |
| Protease inhibitors (PIs) | Lopinavir, darunavir | Block HIV protease (prevents virus maturation) |
| Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) | Dolutegravir, raltegravir | Block integration of viral DNA into host genome |

**India's first-line ART (national programme)**: TDF + 3TC + dolutegravir (TLD) for most adults.

**When to start**: ART is started in ALL HIV-positive individuals regardless of CD4 count (Test and Treat policy).

**PMTCT** (Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission): ART given to HIV+ pregnant women throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding; infant prophylaxis with nevirapine; promote safe infant feeding.

### Nursing care for HIV/AIDS

- **Infection prevention**: standard precautions always; treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious; needle-stick management (wash site, report, post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 hours).
- **Medication adherence**: ART must be taken every day without interruption — missing doses causes resistance. Counsel on importance, timing, storage, side effects.
- **Nutritional support**: high-protein diet; treat opportunistic infections causing weight loss; nutritional supplements.
- **Psychosocial care**: HIV carries stigma and discrimination; ensure confidentiality; support disclosure to partners; link to support groups.
- **Palliative care**: in advanced AIDS; pain management, spiritual and psychosocial support.
- **Prevention counselling**: condom use, harm reduction for IVDU (needle exchange, opioid substitution therapy), partner notification, PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) for high-risk individuals.
- **Occupational exposure (needle-stick)**: wash thoroughly with soap and water; do not squeeze; report to occupational health; risk assessment; PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) with ART must start within 72 hours and continue for 28 days.

---

## 9.3 Tuberculosis (TB)

**TB** is caused by **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**, an acid-fast bacillus (AFB) spread by **airborne** droplet nuclei.

### Pathogenesis
Inhaled droplets → primary complex (Ghon focus — small area of consolidation + hilar lymph nodes; Ghon complex); most cases are contained by immune system; latent TB infection (LTBI); reactivation occurs when immunity falls (HIV, malnutrition, diabetes, old age, immunosuppressants).

**Active pulmonary TB**: cough >3 weeks, blood-stained sputum (haemoptysis), night sweats, fever, weight loss (classic "consumption"), fatigue. Extrapulmonary TB: lymph nodes (most common extrapulmonary), pleura, spine (Pott's disease), meningitis, kidney, intestine, miliary (disseminated).

### Diagnosis
- **Sputum smear microscopy (AFB smear)**: quick, cheap, identifies infectious cases; 3 smears (early morning sputum best).
- **Sputum culture** (Löwenstein–Jensen medium): gold standard but takes 4–8 weeks; needed for drug sensitivity testing.
- **CBNAAT / Xpert MTB/RIF**: rapid PCR — detects TB and rifampicin resistance in 2 hours; preferred initial test.
- **Chest X-ray**: upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, pleural effusion.
- **Mantoux (tuberculin skin test)**: inject 5 TU PPD intradermally; read induration at 48–72 h; >10 mm = positive in most patients; indicates infection but not active disease.
- **IGRA (interferon-gamma release assay)**: blood test, more specific than Mantoux.

### Treatment — DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment Short-course)

**Principle**: every dose supervised by a health worker to ensure adherence. **National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP)** in India uses daily regimens under Nikshay portal.

**Standard regimen (DS-TB)**:

| Phase | Duration | Drugs | Mnemonic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intensive phase | 2 months | Isoniazid (H) + Rifampicin (R) + Pyrazinamide (Z) + Ethambutol (E) | HRZE × 2 months |
| Continuation phase | 4 months | Isoniazid (H) + Rifampicin (R) | HR × 4 months |

Total: 6 months (2HRZE/4HR).

**Drug adverse effects**

| Drug | Key adverse effect | Nursing point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Isoniazid (H) | Peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine), hepatitis | Give pyridoxine (B6) with isoniazid; check LFT |
| Rifampicin (R) | Orange-red discolouration of urine, tears, sweat; hepatitis; drug interactions | Warn patient about colour change; monitor LFT |
| Pyrazinamide (Z) | Hepatitis, hyperuricaemia, arthralgia | LFT; check uric acid; give with food |
| Ethambutol (E) | Optic neuritis (blurred vision, red–green colour blindness) | Monthly visual acuity; report any visual change |

**Drug-resistant TB**: MDR-TB = resistant to H and R; XDR-TB = MDR + resistant to fluoroquinolones and injectable drugs. Longer, more toxic regimens (18–24 months); bedaquiline-based newer regimens.

### Nursing care for TB
- **Airborne precautions**: isolate in a single room with negative pressure if available; N95 mask for healthcare workers; surgical mask for patient when outside room.
- **DOTS**: directly observe every dose; record on treatment card; encourage adherence (explain that incomplete treatment causes resistance and relapse).
- **Nutritional support**: TB is a wasting disease; high-protein, high-calorie diet; Nikshay Poshan Yojana (nutritional support).
- **Contact tracing**: examine all close contacts (household, workplace) for symptoms and Mantoux; treat LTBI if identified.
- **Educate**: cover cough, dispose sputum safely (sputum cup with lid + disinfectant), hand hygiene, complete 6-month course.
- **Monitor side effects**: monthly check of vision (ethambutol), LFT at baseline and monthly (all drugs).
- **HIV testing**: all TB patients should be offered HIV testing (TB-HIV co-infection is common).

---

## 9.4 Viral hepatitis

**Hepatitis** is inflammation of the liver. The five main hepatitis viruses differ in route of transmission and outcome.

| Feature | Hepatitis A (HAV) | Hepatitis B (HBV) | Hepatitis C (HCV) | Hepatitis D (HDV) | Hepatitis E (HEV) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Transmission | Faeco-oral | Blood/body fluids, sexual, MTCT | Blood/body fluids | Needs HBV (co-infection or superinfection) | Faeco-oral |
| Incubation | 15–50 days | 45–180 days | 15–150 days | Similar to HBV | 15–60 days |
| Chronicity | No | Yes (~10% adults, ~90% neonates) | Yes (~80%) | Yes (superinfection) | No (except in immunocompromised) |
| Cirrhosis / cancer | No | Yes (long-term) | Yes (long-term) | Accelerated liver disease | Rarely |
| Vaccine | Yes | Yes | No | HBV vaccination protects | Yes (India — vaccine available) |
| Treatment | Supportive | Tenofovir, entecavir | DAAs (sofosbuvir, daclatasvir) — >95% cure | Treat HBV | Supportive; ribavirin in severe HEV |

**Clinical features** (all types): anorexia, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, right upper quadrant pain, then jaundice (yellow sclera and skin), dark urine (bilirubin), pale stools (less bile reaching gut), hepatomegaly.

**Severe hepatitis B prevention (3-dose HBV vaccine)**: universal infant vaccination in India (at birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks under UIP); healthcare workers must be vaccinated; HBsAg-positive mothers' babies receive HBV vaccine + hepatitis B immunoglobulin within 12 hours of birth.

**Nursing care**
- Bed rest during acute phase; activity as tolerated.
- High-carbohydrate, low-fat diet; small frequent meals; avoid alcohol completely.
- Faeco-oral infections (A, E): hand hygiene, safe water, sanitation, food hygiene.
- Blood-borne infections (B, C): standard precautions, do not share razors, toothbrushes, needles; condom use.
- Monitor for fulminant hepatic failure: altered consciousness, coagulopathy (PT prolonged), hypoglycaemia → refer to ICU.
- Medication precaution: hepatitis patients should avoid hepatotoxic drugs (paracetamol at high dose, NSAIDs, herbal medicines metabolised by the liver).

## 9.5 Malaria

**Malaria** is caused by *Plasmodium* species transmitted by the bite of a female *Anopheles* mosquito.

| Species | Key feature |
| --- | --- |
| P. falciparum | Most dangerous; causes cerebral malaria; can kill |
| P. vivax | Dormant liver stage (hypnozoites); relapses; most common in India |
| P. malariae | Quartan fever (every 72 h); can cause nephrotic syndrome |
| P. ovale | Rare; like vivax, needs radical cure |

**Life cycle (simplified)**:
Mosquito injects sporozoites → liver (pre-erythrocytic stage, 7–30 days) → merozoites released → infect red blood cells → erythrocytic cycle (synchronised rupture of RBCs releases merozoites and toxins → fever spike). Gametocytes taken by mosquito → sexual cycle in mosquito.

**Clinical features**: cyclical fever with chills and rigors (tertian = every 48 h for falciparum/vivax; quartan = every 72 h), headache, myalgia, anaemia (RBC destruction), jaundice, splenomegaly.

**Severe falciparum malaria** (medical emergency): cerebral malaria (impaired consciousness, seizures), severe anaemia, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, hypoglycaemia, blackwater fever (massive haemolysis, haemoglobin in urine).

**Diagnosis**: peripheral blood smear (thick and thin films — gold standard, identifies species and density), Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT — rapid, field use), PCR (research/reference).

**Treatment**

| Species | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Uncomplicated P. falciparum | Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT): artesunate + sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine (AS-SP) in India |
| Uncomplicated P. vivax | Chloroquine + primaquine (primaquine for radical cure; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency — test first) |
| Severe malaria | IV artesunate (preferred) or IV quinine; ICU care |

**Nursing care**: tepid sponging for fever, anti-pyretics (paracetamol — not aspirin in children), fluid balance monitoring, blood glucose monitoring (hypoglycaemia in severe falciparum), neurological observations (cerebral malaria), convulsion precautions, insecticide-treated bed net at night, vector control (remove stagnant water), complete antimalarial course.

---

## 9.6 Typhoid fever

**Typhoid** is caused by **Salmonella typhi** (enteric fever), transmitted via the **faeco-oral route** (contaminated food and water). **Paratyphoid** is caused by S. paratyphi.

**Features**: incubation 10–14 days; stepwise rising fever, bradycardia (relative to fever), headache, malaise; at the end of week 1 → **rose spots** (faint salmon-coloured maculopapular rash on abdomen and chest, transient, appear in crops). Hepatosplenomegaly. Week 2–3: complications.

**Complications**: intestinal perforation (most dangerous — sudden severe abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, shock), intestinal haemorrhage, encephalopathy, myocarditis.

**Diagnosis**: blood culture (best in first week — most sensitive), Widal test (antibodies to O and H antigens; a rising titre is more meaningful than a single test; false positives common), stool culture (second week+), urine culture, TUBEX/Typhidot rapid tests.

**Treatment**: fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) but resistance is increasing; ceftriaxone IV (for severe cases); azithromycin; chloramphenicol (older, side effects — aplastic anaemia).

**Nursing care**: isolation (enteric precautions — standard precautions + strict hand hygiene after using toilet), complete 10–14 day antibiotic course, high-calorie soft bland diet (semi-solid in recovery), monitor for perforation (sudden worsening of pain, rigid abdomen → emergency laparotomy), fluids, temperature monitoring, bed rest, typhoid vaccine for contacts and high-risk groups (Typbar-TCV for children, Vi-PS for adults), safe drinking water and sanitation.

---

## 9.7 Dengue fever

**Dengue** is caused by dengue virus (DENV 1–4), transmitted by the bite of **Aedes aegypti** mosquito (day-biting; breeds in clean stagnant water — tyres, flower pots, overhead tanks).

**Features**: sudden high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain (pain behind the eyes), severe myalgia and arthralgia ("break-bone fever"), maculopapular rash, mild haemorrhagic manifestations (petechiae, bruising, positive tourniquet test — inflate BP cuff to midpoint between systolic and diastolic for 5 minutes; ≥20 petechiae per square inch = positive).

### Warning signs (progress to severe dengue)
Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion), mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement >2 cm, rising haematocrit with rapid fall in platelet count.

### Classification

| Phase | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Dengue without warning signs | Fever 2–7 days, typical dengue features |
| Dengue with warning signs | Any warning sign above |
| Severe dengue | Severe plasma leakage → dengue shock syndrome; severe bleeding; severe organ impairment (liver, CNS, heart, kidney) |

**Dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF)**: fever + thrombocytopenia (<100,000/µL) + haemoconcentration (haematocrit rise ≥20%) + plasma leakage evidence. Can progress to **dengue shock syndrome** (DSS): hypotension, narrow pulse pressure, cold extremities.

**Diagnosis**: NS1 antigen (early, days 1–5), IgM/IgG antibodies (from day 5), PCR; CBC (falling platelet, rising haematocrit), liver function tests (elevated AST/ALT).

**Treatment**: supportive (no specific antiviral); paracetamol for fever (**avoid aspirin and NSAIDs** — increase bleeding risk); IV fluids for severe dengue/shock; platelet transfusion if <10,000/µL or active bleeding; monitor hourly in severe dengue.

**Nursing care**: hourly vital signs in severe dengue, urine output, monitor haematocrit and platelet daily, IV access, fluid resuscitation as ordered (avoid over-hydration), watch for bleeding (gums, nose, IV sites, melaena), no IM injections (bleeding risk), vector control education (remove water-holding containers, use insect repellent, long sleeves, mosquito nets), dengue vaccine (Dengvaxia) available in some countries for seropositive individuals.

## 9.8 Other communicable diseases — brief notes

| Disease | Cause | Transmission | Key nursing point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cholera | Vibrio cholerae | Faeco-oral, contaminated water | Profuse "rice-water" stools; rapid dehydration; oral rehydration solution (ORS) or IV fluids; oral cholera vaccine |
| Rabies | Rabies virus | Animal bite (dogs, bats) | Wash wound with soap and water for 15 minutes; rabies immunoglobulin into wound + rabies vaccine post-exposure; 100% fatal once symptoms start |
| Meningococcal meningitis | Neisseria meningitidis | Droplet | Meningeal signs, petechial rash; IV penicillin; droplet precautions; vaccinate contacts |
| Chickenpox (varicella) | Varicella-zoster virus | Airborne | Vesicular rash, all stages simultaneously; aciclovir for severe cases; airborne + contact precautions; varicella vaccine |
| Measles | Paramyxovirus | Airborne | Koplik's spots (oral), maculopapular rash from face downward; vitamin A; MMR vaccine; airborne precautions |

---

## 9.9 Remember

- Chain of infection: break it at any link (hand hygiene is the simplest and most effective).
- Airborne precautions (N95 mask, single room): TB, measles, chickenpox.
- HIV window period: 3–6 weeks; U=U (undetectable = untransmittable on ART).
- HIV needle-stick: wash, report, PEP within 72 hours.
- TB treatment: 2HRZE/4HR under DOTS; never stop early; orange urine with rifampicin is normal.
- Hepatitis A/E: faeco-oral; B/C: blood/body fluids; B → cirrhosis → cancer; cure HCV with DAAs.
- Malaria diagnosis: blood smear; falciparum = cerebral malaria; radical cure (primaquine) for vivax.
- Typhoid complication to fear: intestinal perforation (rigid abdomen = emergency).
- Dengue: Aedes aegypti; avoid aspirin; platelet fall + haematocrit rise = severe dengue; no IM injections.
- Tourniquet test: ≥20 petechiae per square inch = positive for dengue.
